title: How Oncolytic Viruses Turn Tumors into Immune Targets
summary: An explanatory essay for curious readers who don’t have a virology or immunology background, with the molecular detail left in.
body:
1. The idea in plain words

An oncolytic virus is a virus that grows well in cancer cells and badly in healthy ones. “Oncolytic” just means tumor-dissolving. For a long time the story people told was simple: the virus gets into a tumor cell, makes copies of itself, bursts the cell open, the copies infect the neighbors, and the tumor melts away like ice under a heat lamp.

That story turned out to be mostly wrong, or at least badly incomplete. In most patients the virus simply doesn’t kill enough tumor directly to explain what’s seen. A virus injected into one skin lesion sometimes shrinks lesions elsewhere that never got a needle. Tumors regress weeks after the virus has been cleared. And the best clinical results tend to show up when the virus is paired with antibodies that block immune checkpoints, drugs that do nothing except free T cells to do their job. The modern view, set out in reviews by Russell, Peng and Bell (2012), Lichty and colleagues (2014) and Kaufman, Kohlhapp and Zloza (2015), is that the virus works mainly as a way of starting an immune response inside the tumor. The virus lights the match. The immune system does most of the burning.

Why would a tumor need that kind of help? Because the immune system often sees tumors and fails to react. Tumors are built from our own cells. They carry mutated proteins that could in principle be recognized as foreign, but they present them quietly, with none of the danger signals that normally tell the body to act, and they surround themselves with cells that actively calm the immune system down. Immunologists call a tumor like that “cold.” A viral infection is the opposite of quiet. It’s loud, inflammatory, and full of molecular patterns that animals have been trained by hundreds of millions of years of evolution to treat as an emergency. An oncolytic virus drops the tumor’s antigens into the middle of that emergency.

Chen and Mellman (2013) described the chain of events a successful anticancer immune response has to complete: antigens are released from dying tumor cells, dendritic cells pick them up and mature, T cells are primed in lymph nodes, travel to the tumor, get inside, recognize the cancer cells and kill them, which releases more antigen and restarts the cycle. Most cancer drugs touch one link in that chain. Oncolytic viruses can push on several at once, which is a large part of why people find them interesting.

The rest of this essay follows the chain. First a little history, then the evolutionary reasons tumors are vulnerable to viruses in the first place, then the immunology step by step: how the infected cell sounds the alarm, how it dies in a way the immune system notices, how T cells get primed, and how the tumor neighborhood gets rebuilt. After that there’s a tour of the individual viruses that have actually been put into patients, a look at how they’ve been engineered and combined with other drugs, and a frank section on where they fail.

2. A short history, because it explains the design

People noticed long before anyone knew what a virus was that cancers sometimes shrink during infections. The first well-known report involving a deliberately given virus came from Dock (1904), who described a woman with cervical cancer who improved after receiving a rabies vaccine. Through the mid-twentieth century there were scattered reports of leukemia remitting after infections (Pelner, Fowler and Nauts 1958), and a famous case of a Burkitt lymphoma regressing during measles (Bluming and Ziegler 1971). Kelly and Russell (2007) give a thorough account of how this slowly turned into a field.

The early attempts, in the 1950s and 1960s, used wild viruses given to patients with advanced cancer. Some people did respond, but the results were unpredictable and sometimes dangerous, and the patients’ own antibodies cleared the virus quickly. The idea went quiet for decades.

What revived it was genetic engineering. Martuza and colleagues (1991) deleted the thymidine kinase gene from herpes simplex virus (HSV) so that it could only replicate in dividing cells, and showed it shrank human glioma in mice. Bischoff and colleagues (1996) reported an adenovirus lacking the E1B-55K gene that, they argued, grew selectively in cells with defective p53, and the virus (ONYX-015) went into clinical trials (Heise et al. 1997). Coffey and colleagues (1998) found that reovirus, a mild virus that infects people without much fuss, replicated in cells with an activated Ras pathway. And Stojdl and colleagues (2000) showed that vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) was crippled in normal cells but flourished in cells with defects in the interferon response. Each of these papers made the same point from a different angle: cancer cells have lost defenses that normal cells keep, and a virus can be chosen or built to exploit the gap.

The first products reached the market in an uneven way. Rigvir, an unmodified ECHO-7 enterovirus, was registered in Latvia in 2004 for melanoma (Alberts et al. 2018). It was later withdrawn, and the evidence behind it has been debated. H101 (Oncorine), an adenovirus related to ONYX-015, was approved in China in 2005 for head and neck cancer in combination with chemotherapy (Garber 2006; Liang 2018). The first approval by the US Food and Drug Administration came in 2015 for talimogene laherparepvec, or T-VEC, an HSV engineered to carry the gene for GM-CSF, after a randomized phase 3 trial in melanoma (Andtbacka et al. 2015; Rehman et al. 2016). Japan gave conditional approval in 2021 to teserpaturev (Delytact, also called G47Δ), another engineered HSV, for malignant glioma (Todo et al. 2022; Frampton 2022).

The newest chapter is still being written as this essay goes out. In August 2026 the FDA granted accelerated approval to vusolimogene oderparepvec (RP1, brand name Tudriqev) together with nivolumab for advanced melanoma that has progressed after anti-PD-1 therapy. That approval came after two earlier complete response letters, in July 2025 and April 2026, which were driven by concerns about whether a single-arm trial can show effectiveness, and after an advisory committee vote of 10 to 3 in favor on July 30, 2026. The approval is conditional on a confirmatory randomized trial, IGNYTE-3, that is still running. A bladder cancer virus, cretostimogene grenadenorepvec, has had its application filed in pieces, with the company expecting to finish the submission in the fourth quarter of 2026. Neither of these outcomes is the final word on whether oncolytic viruses will become a standard pillar of cancer care, and the section on limits below explains why.

3. Why a tumor is vulnerable: the evolutionary view

It helps to think of a tumor not as a lump of sick tissue but as a population of cells evolving under selection. Hanahan and Weinberg (2011) listed the abilities that successful cancers acquire: sustained growth signaling, evasion of growth suppressors, resistance to cell death, and avoidance of immune destruction among them. Schreiber, Old and Smyth (2011) described how the immune system itself prunes tumor populations, killing the visible clones and leaving the quieter ones, so that tumors that survive to be diagnosed have often been through an immunological filter. Evolution is opportunistic, and every adaptation costs something. The oncolytic virus is built to exploit those costs.

3.1 The price of switching off the interferon system

Interferons are the body’s chemical emergency broadcast. A cell that detects a virus makes type I interferons (IFN-α and IFN-β), which tell it and its neighbors to shut down protein synthesis, degrade viral RNA, and raise the cell’s defenses. They also do something that matters for cancer: they slow cell division and boost antigen presentation, so interferon signaling is an anti-tumor pathway as well as an antiviral one (Parker, Rautela and Hertzog 2016). A growing tumor therefore has a reason to weaken it. Critchley-Thorne and colleagues (2009) found that impaired interferon signaling is a common defect in human cancers. That’s a good trade for the tumor in the short term. It’s a bad trade the moment a virus turns up, because the cell has lost its main way of saying “stop, I’m infected.” This is the trick that Stojdl and colleagues (2000, 2003) exploited with VSV, and it’s why interferon-defective tumor cells are a recurring theme in the whole field.

3.2 Pathways that viruses evolved to hijack are already broken

Many viruses have evolved ways to push the cell into a state where it makes copies of the viral genome. Adenovirus does it with its E1A protein, which binds the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) and releases the E2F transcription factors that drive the cell into DNA synthesis, and with E1B-55K, which was thought to neutralize p53. In a normal cell the virus must do this work itself. In a cancer cell that has already lost Rb control or p53 function, the work is partly done, so a virus that no longer carries its own Rb-binding or p53-binding function can still replicate in the tumor and not in healthy tissue. That’s the logic behind ONYX-015 (Bischoff et al. 1996; Heise et al. 1997), the Rb-pathway-targeted DNX-2401 (also called Delta-24-RGD; Fueyo et al. 2000) and the bladder cancer virus cretostimogene, which puts the viral replication gene under an E2F-responsive promoter. In fairness, the original p53 story for ONYX-015 was later complicated: O’Shea and colleagues (2004) argued that the real source of its tumor selectivity was late viral RNA export, not p53 status. Biology rarely stays as tidy as the first paper makes it sound.

The same reasoning applies to Ras. Active Ras signaling in tumors suppresses the PKR antiviral kinase, which would otherwise shut down translation in an infected cell. Reovirus exploits exactly that (Coffey et al. 1998; Strong et al. 1998). Poxviruses and vaccinia in particular grow well in cells with activated EGFR–Ras signaling (Parato et al. 2012), and vaccinia carries its own thymidine kinase, so versions that lack it depend on the high nucleotide pools of dividing cells (Buller et al. 1985).

There’s a second layer: some tumors also display more of the molecules viruses use as doors. High CD46 on many cancers invites the measles vaccine strain (Anderson et al. 2004). ICAM-1 and DAF (CD55) on melanoma and other tumors let coxsackievirus A21 in (Shafren et al. 2004). CD155, the poliovirus receptor, is heavily expressed in glioblastoma and is the reason an engineered poliovirus was tested there (Desjardins et al. 2018). Seneca Valley virus uses the anthrax toxin receptor ANTXR1 (also called TEM8), found on some tumors and tumor vasculature (Miles et al. 2017).

3.3 An arms race, run backwards

Viruses and their hosts have been in a coevolutionary conflict for as long as either has existed. Hosts evolve restriction factors and sensors, viruses evolve ways to switch them off, and the cycle repeats (Daugherty and Malik 2012; Duggal and Emerman 2012). Randall and Goodbourn (2008) catalogue the staggering number of ways that viruses block interferon induction and signaling. Herpesviruses have the ICP34.5 protein, which pulls a phosphatase onto the PKR target eIF2α so that the cell can’t shut down translation (Chou et al. 1990; He, Gross and Roizman 1997). They also make ICP47, which blocks the TAP transporter and so keeps viral peptides off MHC class I molecules (the cell’s display shelf for T cells). Poxviruses carry a large collection of decoy receptors and inhibitors for cytokines, interferons and complement (Smith et al. 2013).

Oncolytic virus design runs this arms race backwards. Delete the viral counter-measures and the virus becomes a wimp in normal cells, which still have intact interferon responses and kill it quickly. In a tumor cell whose own defenses are already compromised, the same deletions cost the virus little. The nice side effect is immunological. Deleting ICP47 from HSV not only reduces neurovirulence-independent immune evasion; it allows MHC class I to function normally so tumor and viral peptides can be displayed to T cells (Todo et al. 2001). It also leads to earlier expression of another HSV gene, US11, which partly rescues the replication lost when ICP34.5 is deleted. Both T-VEC and G47Δ carry that deletion. In other words, the virus has been edited so that it is both safer and easier for the immune system to see.

3.4 Alarm systems older than the immune system

The sensing machinery that oncolytic viruses trigger is very ancient. The cGAS–STING pathway, which detects DNA in the wrong place, has relatives in bacteria, where related systems defend against phages (Morehouse et al. 2020). The RIG-I and Toll-like receptor families are similarly old in animal evolution. Adaptive immunity, with its B and T cells, is a comparatively late addition. This matters for the story: a virus is a stimulus the old, fast innate system understands extremely well, and that system is what turns on the newer adaptive system. The virus is, in effect, using an old language to talk the newer, more specific cells into paying attention to a tumor.

3.5 Tumors carry fossils of viruses

Human genomes are full of the remains of ancient retroviral infections. Endogenous retroviruses make up about eight percent of our DNA and are usually kept silent by epigenetic marks. Two groups showed in 2015 that when tumor cells are treated with DNA-demethylating drugs, those sequences wake up and make double-stranded RNA, which the cell’s own RNA sensors read as infection, triggering interferon (Chiappinelli et al. 2015; Roulois et al. 2015). They called the effect viral mimicry. It’s relevant here because it shows that tumor cells can be pushed into a virus-like state without a real virus, and that the sensing machinery is intact in many of them. An oncolytic virus pushes the same button, only harder and from the outside.

4. From infection to alarm: how the tumor senses the virus

Once a virus is inside a tumor cell it begins to leave a trail that the cell’s sensors can detect. Which sensors fire depends on what kind of virus it is.

Sensors in the cell. For RNA viruses such as VSV, measles, Newcastle disease virus, reovirus and poliovirus, the key sensors are the RIG-I-like receptors, RIG-I and MDA5, which sit in the cytoplasm and recognize double-stranded or 5′-triphosphate RNA (Rehwinkel and Gack 2020). For DNA viruses such as HSV, adenovirus and vaccinia, the key sensor is cGAS, which binds DNA in the cytoplasm and makes the signaling molecule cGAMP, which in turn activates STING (Sun et al. 2013). Toll-like receptors TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 live in endosomes and catch viral nucleic acids that cells have taken up by engulfing debris from other infected cells (Kawai and Akira 2010). All of these pathways converge on a small set of transcription factors, mainly IRF3, IRF7 and NF-κB, which switch on type I interferon genes and a wave of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.

Why this is the part that matters most. It’s tempting to see interferon as just an antiviral defense that tumors use to resist the virus, and in some tumors it is. But in the tumor as a whole it works in the opposite direction. Two papers published together in 2011 showed that type I interferon signaling in dendritic cells, specifically the CD8α+ subset (now called conventional type 1 dendritic cells, cDC1), is needed for the immune rejection of tumors (Diamond et al. 2011; Fuertes et al. 2011). The STING pathway turned out to be the main route by which tumors trigger that interferon response in the first place (Woo et al. 2014; Deng et al. 2014). The oncolytic virus is, among other things, a very efficient STING and RIG-I agonist. In a human trial of an engineered poliovirus, for example, infection produced an interferon-dominated activation of dendritic cells and tumor antigen-specific cytotoxic T cells (Brown et al. 2017).

Chemokines and recruitment. Interferon-stimulated cells release chemokines such as CXCL9, CXCL10 and CCL5. These are the road signs that tell T cells, NK cells and dendritic cells where the action is. Sistigu and colleagues (2014) showed that tumor-cell-autonomous type I interferon signaling, with CXCL10 as a major output, is required for effective anticancer immunity triggered by chemotherapy, and the same wiring is engaged by viruses.

Inflammasomes and other death programs. Some viral infections activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in dendritic cells and other myeloid cells, which cleaves pro-IL-1β into active IL-1β. That cytokine is needed for some forms of anticancer immunity (Ghiringhelli et al. 2009). Infection can also drive infected tumor cells into necroptosis, a form of programmed, inflammatory necrosis, through the RIG-I or STING pathways (Schock et al. 2017). Which type of death results depends on the virus and the cell, but the common thread is that the cell dies loudly.

The immune cells that fight back. The same alarm also summons cells that attack the virus, and this is where the story gets complicated. NK cells are drawn to infected tumors and can kill them, which contributes to tumor control, but in glioblastoma NK cells recognizing the infected cells through the receptors NKp30 and NKp46 were shown to clear the virus early and limit its spread (Alvarez-Breckenridge et al. 2012). Macrophages and microglia can similarly soak up the virus: depleting them raised viral titers in brain tumors (Fulci et al. 2007). Whether an early innate response helps or hurts is a matter of timing, and we’ll come back to it.

5. Dying in a way the immune system notices

Not all cell death is equal. Normal cells die all day long by apoptosis, and the neighboring phagocytes clear them away without raising any fuss. This is called tolerogenic death, and it’s a good thing, because you don’t want your immune system attacking every dying skin cell. Immunogenic cell death (ICD) is the other category: death that is accompanied by signals that tell the immune system to pay attention and remember. Kroemer and colleagues (2013) laid out the concept for cancer therapy, and Galluzzi and colleagues (2020) published consensus guidelines for how to define and measure it.

The central idea is that the immune system responds to antigens plus danger. The antigen alone is usually ignored or tolerated. The antigen with a set of danger signals, which immunologists call damage-associated molecular patterns, or DAMPs, becomes a vaccine. The main DAMPs of ICD are well characterized:

  • Calreticulin is normally inside the endoplasmic reticulum. When it appears on the surface of a dying cell, it works as an “eat me” signal for dendritic cells (Obeid et al. 2007).

  • ATP released from dying cells attracts dendritic cell precursors and, acting on the P2X7 receptor, activates the inflammasome (Ghiringhelli et al. 2009). ATP release depends on autophagy in the dying cell (Michaud et al. 2011).

  • HMGB1, a nuclear protein, is released late in death and stimulates dendritic cells through TLR4, helping them process and present the antigens they’ve taken up (Apetoh et al. 2007).

  • Annexin A1 acts through a receptor on dendritic cells called FPR1 and holds them close to dying tumor cells (Vacchelli et al. 2015).

  • Type I interferon and CXCL10 from the dying cell itself, as above (Sistigu et al. 2014).

Oncolytic viruses can produce most of these, and in the right combinations. Workenhe and Mossman (2014) reviewed how virus infection engages ICD, and subsequent studies have shown calreticulin exposure, ATP and HMGB1 release in cells infected with many different viruses. For example, Newcastle disease virus infection of glioma produced ICD that supported long-term survival and tumor-specific immune memory in mice (Koks et al. 2015). Not every virus triggers every DAMP, and some viruses actively dampen specific ones, so ICD isn’t a binary property of a virus. Isaeva and colleagues (2025) survey how engineering can push viruses toward more immunogenic death.

There are two further points that are easy to miss. One is that the viral infection supplies a second kind of signal that classical chemotherapy-induced ICD lacks: pathogen-associated molecular patterns, the viral nucleic acids and proteins themselves, which light up innate sensors in dendritic cells that have eaten infected tumor debris. The other is that the cells are dying in an environment already full of interferon. Both help the dendritic cells that arrive to switch from a resting, tolerance-inducing state into an activated state able to prime T cells.

Some viruses add a further mechanical twist. Fusogenic proteins, such as the gibbon ape leukemia virus envelope used in RP1, make infected cells fuse with their uninfected neighbors into giant multinucleated syncytia, which spreads the infection and, as the fused cell eventually dies, produces large, dense packages of antigen and DAMPs (Thomas et al. 2019).

6. Priming T cells: from dead tumor cells to a trained army

The cells that connect death to T cell priming are the dendritic cells. Tumor-resident cDC1s are particularly good at cross-presentation, the unusual ability to take up proteins from dead cells and display their peptides on MHC class I, the molecules that CD8+ killer T cells inspect (Joffre et al. 2012). After engulfing infected tumor debris, an activated dendritic cell migrates to a lymph node, where it presents tumor peptides to naive T cells along with the costimulatory signals and cytokines (IL-12 chief among them) that tell the T cell to become a killer rather than to ignore the signal.

Here the unusual strength of oncolytic viruses becomes visible. A T cell response to a viral antigen is easy to start, because viral proteins are foreign and the immune system has no tolerance to them. But the dendritic cells that picked up the debris have also picked up tumor antigens, many of them from the tumor’s own mutated proteins. The T cells that proliferate in response include clones against viral antigens, but also clones against tumor antigens, and that spread of the response from the original target to additional tumor targets is called epitope or antigen spreading. It was seen in mice treated with VSV carrying a cDNA library, where the response against tumor antigens, not the virus, was what drove the cures (Diaz et al. 2007). It was seen in patients with melanoma and other cancers treated with intravenous reovirus (Prestwich et al. 2008), and in preclinical work Woller and colleagues (2015) found that viral infection of tumors broadened the T cell response to neoantigens and overcame resistance to PD-1 blockade.

Patient data are consistent with this. Kaufman and colleagues (2010) reported that intralesional T-VEC in melanoma was associated with local and distant immune responses and with regression of uninjected lesions. The pivotal randomized trial in melanoma showed a higher durable response rate for T-VEC than for GM-CSF injections alone, and responses included uninjected and visceral lesions (Andtbacka et al. 2015). Ribas and colleagues (2017) biopsied tumors from melanoma patients receiving T-VEC and found increased CD8+ T cells, increased PD-L1 expression and an interferon-γ gene signature, even in lesions that had not been injected. Samson and colleagues (2018) gave reovirus intravenously to patients with brain tumors scheduled for surgery and found that it reached the tumor, increased cytotoxic T cell infiltration and increased PD-1 and PD-L1 expression. In recurrent glioma, DNX-2401 injection was followed by CD8+ and T-bet+ cell infiltration and a decrease in the PD-1 and other markers of T cell exhaustion in some patients, alongside a minority of long-term survivors (Lang et al. 2018).

Some of these immune responses outlast the virus. Mice cured of tumors with Newcastle disease virus or the engineered Maraba virus rejected a rechallenge with the same tumor (Koks et al. 2015; Bourgeois-Daigneault et al. 2018), which means a memory population had been established. This is the immunological meaning of “turning the tumor into an immune target”: the tumor’s antigens have been repackaged as a vaccine, and the vaccine keeps working after the virus is gone.

7. Rebuilding the neighborhood: the tumor microenvironment

A tumor is more than cancer cells. It’s a neighborhood with blood vessels, fibroblasts, structural matrix, and a crowd of immune cells, many of them recruited by the tumor to protect it. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) damp down other T cells. Myeloid-derived suppressor cells and tumor-associated macrophages of the “M2” type produce factors like IL-10, TGF-β and arginase that starve and silence killer T cells. Spranger and Gajewski (2018) reviewed how oncogenic signaling inside tumor cells, such as the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, can shut off the chemokines needed to bring T cells in at all. Immunologists call a tumor that resists in these ways “immune excluded” or “immune desert,” and none of these resistance mechanisms will be overcome simply by adding more T cells.

Viral infection changes the neighborhood quickly and in several directions at once.

It changes the chemistry. Interferons, TNF, IL-1β, IL-6 and chemokines pour out of infected and dying cells. The tumor goes from an environment dominated by TGF-β and IL-10 to one dominated by interferon-γ, CXCL9 and CXCL10. Achard and colleagues (2018) describe this as lighting a fire in the tumor microenvironment, which is a fair description of the clinical biopsies: increased CD8+ T cell counts, interferon-γ signatures and PD-L1 expression are repeatedly seen after oncolytic virus injection (Ribas et al. 2017; Samson et al. 2018; Lang et al. 2018).

It changes who is in the room. In glioblastoma models, an HSV armed with IL-12, combined with anti-PD-1, shifted tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory, tumor-fighting state and reduced Tregs, and the macrophage shift was needed for the therapeutic effect (Saha, Martuza and Rabkin 2017). Ilkow and colleagues (2015) reported that interactions between infected tumor cells and immune cells inside the tumor can actually aid viral activity, not just limit it. Their point was that the virus and the host immune cells co-operate in ways that early models, which treated immunity purely as an obstacle, missed.

It changes the plumbing. Many tumors have chaotic, leaky blood vessels that deliver oxygen poorly and impede the entry of T cells. Some viruses, vaccinia in particular, infect tumor endothelial cells, and the resulting inflammation can shut down the tumor’s blood flow, starving the core (Breitbach et al. 2007). That’s a direct kill that doesn’t depend on the cancer cells being infectious at all. It also releases more antigen into a tumor that is now full of inflammatory cells.

It changes the display. Interferon increases the expression of MHC class I and the antigen-processing machinery, so cells that had hidden their antigens begin to show them again. Deletion of the HSV ICP47 gene prevents the virus from undoing that effect (Todo et al. 2001).

It creates a “foreign” target for CD4+ T cells. Viral proteins are strongly immunogenic. CD4+ helper T cells that recognize them release cytokines and license dendritic cells and CD8+ T cells in the tumor, a kind of help that spills over onto the tumor antigens being presented at the same time. This effect is a plausible reason why even viruses with fairly modest direct killing can produce systemic responses, and it fits with the observation that prior immunity to a virus doesn’t always reduce its anticancer effect (Ricca et al. 2018, discussed again below).

Bommareddy, Shettigar and Kaufman (2018) put this together as a model in which oncolytic virus converts a tumor with low T cell infiltration into one with high infiltration and an interferon-rich environment, which is the setting where checkpoint blockade tends to work. We’ll return to that when we reach combination therapy.

8. A field guide to the viruses that have been tried

A lot of different viruses have been put into people. It’s useful to hold them side by side, partly to see how many routes lead to the same result and partly because each has taught the field something. 8.1 Herpes simplex viruses: the workhorse

HSV-1 is a large DNA virus with a lot of non-essential genes, so it can be engineered heavily, and it tolerates large inserts. It infects many cell types, spreads from cell to cell, and has an antiviral drug (aciclovir) that can shut it down if something goes wrong. These practical advantages explain why three approved products belong to this family.

T-VEC is HSV-1 with both copies of ICP34.5 deleted (so it can’t resist PKR in healthy cells), ICP47 deleted, and the human GM-CSF gene inserted (Liu et al. 2003). GM-CSF is a cytokine that attracts and matures dendritic cells, which is why it was chosen. In the randomized phase 3 trial OPTiM, the durable response rate was 16.3 percent with T-VEC against 2.1 percent for GM-CSF injections alone, in patients with unresectable melanoma (Andtbacka et al. 2015). Responses were seen in uninjected lesions, which is the evidence for systemic immunity. The follow-up combination studies are instructive. A phase 1b trial of T-VEC with pembrolizumab in melanoma reported a high response rate and correlated responses with CD8+ T cell infiltration and interferon-γ signaling in tumors (Ribas et al. 2017). T-VEC with ipilimumab showed higher response rates than ipilimumab alone in a randomized phase 2 trial (Chesney et al. 2018; Puzanov et al. 2016). But the confirmatory phase 3 trial, MASTERKEY-265, comparing T-VEC plus pembrolizumab with pembrolizumab alone, did not show a significant improvement in progression-free or overall survival (Chesney et al. 2023). This is an important and sobering result. A combination that looked wonderful in early studies didn’t clear the bar in a large randomized trial, and it’s one reason the field has become more cautious about early-phase response rates.

G47Δ carries three alterations: ICP34.5 and ICP47 deletions as in T-VEC, plus inactivation of ICP6, the viral ribonucleotide reductase, which makes it depend on cellular enzymes that are plentiful in dividing cells (Todo et al. 2001). The ICP47 deletion leads to early expression of US11 and improved MHC class I presentation. In a phase 2 trial in residual or recurrent glioblastoma, patients injected repeatedly into the tumor had a one-year survival that compared favorably with historical controls, and the trial led to conditional approval in Japan (Todo et al. 2022). Because it was a single-arm trial, the same caveat applies that later affected RP1 in the United States.

RP1 takes a different approach to immunogenicity. It adds a fusogenic protein, a modified gibbon ape leukemia virus envelope glycoprotein (GALV-GP R−), plus GM-CSF, on a clinical HSV-1 strain with ICP34.5 and ICP47 deleted (Thomas et al. 2019). Cells infected with RP1 fuse with neighboring cells into syncytia, which spreads the virus and, as discussed above, increases the amount of antigen and DAMPs released on death. The approval in August 2026 was for use with nivolumab in adults with unresectable melanoma that had progressed on anti-PD-1 therapy, based on response rate and response duration in the single-arm IGNYTE trial. The FDA’s accelerated pathway means continued approval depends on the confirmatory phase 3 trial, IGNYTE-3. It’s a reasonable bet that the reasoning will be watched closely, since this is the group of patients, those who have stopped responding to checkpoint blockade, where a virus that reawakens T cell infiltration has the clearest rationale.

8.2 Adenoviruses: the Rb story

Adenovirus is a DNA virus with a small genome, a well-understood replication cycle and efficient entry via the coxsackie and adenovirus receptor and integrins. Many people have antibodies against it, which makes systemic delivery difficult but doesn’t prevent injections directly into tumors or into the bladder.

H101 (Oncorine), related to ONYX-015, has deletions in E1B-55K and part of E3. It was approved in China in 2005 for use with chemotherapy in nasopharyngeal and other head and neck cancers (Garber 2006; Liang 2018). Its approval was based on trials that would now be considered small by Western regulatory standards, and it has been very little studied outside China.

DNX-2401 (Delta-24-RGD) has a 24-base-pair deletion in E1A that removes the Rb-binding site, so it can only replicate in cells where Rb control has been lost, and an RGD peptide in its fiber so that it can enter cells through integrins, which are abundant on glioma cells (Fueyo et al. 2000). In a phase 1 trial in recurrent glioma, a subset of patients had long-term survival, and post-treatment biopsies showed immune cell infiltration, including CD8+ and T-bet+ cells, along with signs of reduced PD-1 expression (Lang et al. 2018). It has since been combined with pembrolizumab.

Cretostimogene grenadenorepvec (CG0070) is an adenovirus in which the E1A gene is controlled by the E2F-1 promoter, so it only replicates in cells with a disrupted Rb pathway, which is common in bladder cancer, and which also carries GM-CSF (Burke et al. 2012). It’s delivered into the bladder, where it contacts the tumor directly. In the BOND-003 trial in BCG-unresponsive high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer with carcinoma in situ, the company has reported a complete response at any time in about three-quarters of patients, with a 24-month complete response rate of 41.8 percent and no grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events in the reported data (CG Oncology 2025, 2026). These figures are from company reports and conference presentations of a single-arm trial, and a rolling application to the FDA is due to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026.

It’s worth separating these from nadofaragene firadenovec (Adstiladrin), an adenovirus that can’t replicate and just delivers the gene for interferon-α2b to bladder cells. It’s not an oncolytic virus, but it gets at the same immunological idea from a different direction, by making the bladder tumor make its own interferon. It was tested in BCG-unresponsive bladder cancer (Boorjian et al. 2021) and was approved by the FDA in late 2022.

8.3 Poxviruses: built for the bloodstream

Vaccinia, the virus used for the smallpox vaccine, is a large DNA virus that replicates entirely in the cytoplasm (so it never enters the nucleus and is safe from integrating into the genome), spreads rapidly between cells and travels in the bloodstream. It has more immune-evasion proteins than almost any other virus (Smith et al. 2013).

Pexa-Vec (JX-594) is a Wyeth-strain vaccinia lacking thymidine kinase and carrying GM-CSF. Breitbach and colleagues (2011) showed in a phase 1 trial that intravenous Pexa-Vec could reach and replicate in tumors in different organs, and that it induced an anti-tumor immune response in some patients. A randomized phase 2 trial in liver cancer by Heo and colleagues (2013) suggested a dose-related survival advantage. The phase 3 trial, PHOCUS, which combined Pexa-Vec with sorafenib in liver cancer, was stopped after an interim analysis in 2019 indicated that it was unlikely to meet its survival endpoint. Vaccinia’s failure there is probably a reminder that intravenous delivery remains hard: antibodies, complement and platelets in the blood all stand between the virus and the tumor (Ferguson, Lemoine and Wang 2012).

8.4 Reovirus: the unmodified virus

Reovirus is a harmless virus (the name stands for respiratory enteric orphan virus, because for a long time it wasn’t linked to a disease) with ten segments of double-stranded RNA. Pelareorep (Reolysin) is an unmodified type 3 Dearing strain. Its tumor selectivity depends on Ras activation and PKR suppression (Coffey et al. 1998; Strong et al. 1998). Its immunology is among the best characterized. Reovirus activates human dendritic cells directly and makes them stimulate NK and T cell responses (Errington et al. 2008), and in patients it primes adaptive anti-tumor immunity (Prestwich et al. 2008). In brain tumor patients given reovirus intravenously, the virus reached the tumor and the T cell response and PD-1/PD-L1 up-regulation it triggered suggested a rationale for combining with checkpoint inhibitors (Samson et al. 2018). In a randomized phase 2 trial in metastatic breast cancer, adding pelareorep to weekly paclitaxel suggested an overall survival benefit though progression-free survival was not significantly different (Bernstein et al. 2018). No approval has resulted yet.

8.5 Picornaviruses: poliovirus, coxsackievirus, Seneca Valley, ECHO-7

These are small, non-enveloped RNA viruses that replicate very quickly in the cytoplasm.

PVSRIPO is the Sabin type 1 poliovirus vaccine strain in which the viral IRES (the sequence that lets the virus start translation) has been replaced with that of a human rhinovirus, which prevents it from growing in neurons but still allows it to grow in tumor cells that express the poliovirus receptor CD155. In mouse studies, infection of tumor cells and dendritic cells led to a strong, interferon-dominant activation of dendritic cells and tumor antigen-specific T cells, and the response persisted even when infected tumor cells were not killed efficiently (Brown et al. 2017). In recurrent glioblastoma, intratumoral PVSRIPO produced a survival curve that leveled off for a subset of patients, compared with historical controls (Desjardins et al. 2018).

Coxsackievirus A21 (CVA21, or V937) uses ICAM-1 and DAF, which are expressed on melanoma and other tumors (Shafren et al. 2004). Intratumoral CVA21 showed clinical activity in melanoma (Andtbacka et al. 2021), and it’s being developed together with checkpoint inhibitors.

Seneca Valley virus (SVV-001) was found by chance as a contaminant in cell culture and turned out to infect neuroendocrine tumor cells through ANTXR1 (Miles et al. 2017). A phase 1 study showed it was safe given intravenously and could replicate in tumors (Rudin et al. 2011). Rigvir, the ECHO-7 enterovirus registered in Latvia, remains controversial and its supporting evidence has been described as thin (Alberts et al. 2018).

8.6 Measles, Newcastle disease virus, and the paramyxoviruses

Measles vaccine strains infect cells through CD46, which is overexpressed on many tumor types, and cause cells to fuse into syncytia (Anderson et al. 2004). Genetically modified measles virus expressing the carcinoembryonic antigen was tolerated when infused into the abdomen in women with recurrent ovarian cancer (Galanis et al. 2010). A single high-dose intravenous infusion of measles virus engineered to carry the sodium iodide symporter, which lets the infected cells be imaged and also be targeted with radioiodine, was followed by a durable remission of multiple myeloma in one patient (Russell et al. 2014), a case that showed it was possible for systemic virotherapy to clear disseminated disease, though it has not been widely reproduced.

Newcastle disease virus (NDV) is an avian paramyxovirus that is generally harmless to humans. It has been used in cancer research for decades. Schirrmacher (2016) reviewed fifty years of clinical use, mostly as modified tumor cell vaccines in Germany. The intravenous NDV strain PV701 was tested in a phase 1 trial in advanced solid cancers (Pecora et al. 2002). Preclinical work has shown that NDV in a melanoma model induces local immune changes and makes the tumor sensitive to CTLA-4 blockade, not just in the injected tumor but also in a distant uninjected one (Zamarin et al. 2014). Koks and colleagues (2015) found that NDV in glioma produced ICD, long-term survival and tumor-specific immune memory.

8.7 Rhabdoviruses: VSV and Maraba

VSV is a livestock virus that is mild in humans, and it was the first virus where interferon defects were shown to be the basis of cancer selectivity (Stojdl et al. 2000, 2003). Hastie and Grdzelishvili (2012) review its engineering. VSV carrying a cDNA library from normal tissue was a useful tool for showing that tumor antigens could be targeted by the response (Diaz et al. 2007). A newer construct, VSV-IFNβ, carries interferon-β to protect normal tissue and stimulate immunity. Maraba virus was identified in a screen of rhabdoviruses for potency against cancer cell lines and then attenuated into MG1 (Brun et al. 2010). Bourgeois-Daigneault and colleagues (2018) showed that giving MG1 before surgery in mouse models of triple-negative breast cancer, a so-called neoadjuvant approach, primed the immune system to prevent metastatic recurrence and made the tumors sensitive to checkpoint therapy. That study is part of the reason neoadjuvant virotherapy, in which virus is injected before the tumor is removed rather than after, has attracted interest.

8.8 Parvoviruses

H-1 parvovirus is a rat virus with a small single-stranded DNA genome that replicates in rapidly dividing cells and doesn’t cause human disease. In a first phase 1/2a trial in recurrent glioblastoma, it was safe and produced signs of immune activity within the tumor, including T cell infiltration and markers of immunogenic cell death (Geletneky et al. 2017).

9. Better weapons and better partners: arming and combining

Once it was clear that the immune response was doing much of the work, the design question changed. Instead of asking how to make a virus kill faster, people began asking how to make it a better immune adjuvant, and what to give with it.

9.1 Arming the virus

Because many oncolytic viruses can carry extra genes, they can be used to deliver immune-stimulating proteins directly inside the tumor, at a concentration that would be toxic if given into the blood. Several families of payloads have been tried.

  • Cytokines and growth factors. GM-CSF is the most common, used in T-VEC, Pexa-Vec, RP1 and cretostimogene, on the logic that it recruits and matures dendritic cells. Interestingly, how much it actually contributes is not clear, and Kaufman and colleagues (2015) note that evidence for its added value is mixed. IL-12, a powerful driver of Th1 and killer T cell responses, has been used in HSV vectors with striking results in mouse glioma (Saha et al. 2017). Interferon-β is carried by VSV-IFNβ to protect normal tissue and promote immunity.

  • Costimulatory ligands. An adenovirus encoding CD40 ligand, which activates dendritic cells directly, produced immune-dependent tumor control in mouse models (Diaconu et al. 2012).

  • Antibodies against checkpoints. Adenoviruses have been built to make a fully human anti-CTLA-4 antibody inside the tumor (Dias et al. 2012). Localized production avoids the immune-related side effects of giving the same antibody systemically, at least in principle.

  • Bispecific T cell engagers. These are small proteins that link a T cell, through CD3, to a tumor surface protein and force contact between them. An oncolytic adenovirus that made an EpCAM-targeted engager caused T cells in patient tumor samples to kill cancer cells (Freedman et al. 2017).

  • Fusogenic proteins. As described for RP1, these make infected cells fuse with their neighbors, which spreads the infection and increases the immunogenicity of cell death (Thomas et al. 2019).

There’s a limit to how much cargo a virus can carry and how long its genes keep making protein before the cell dies, and arming a virus with immune stimulators can sometimes speed up its own clearance. The strategy works best when the payload does something that the virus alone can’t.

9.2 Pairing with checkpoint inhibitors

Checkpoint inhibitors are antibodies against PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4, molecular brakes on T cells. They work well in tumors that already contain T cells that recognize the cancer, and poorly in tumors that don’t. Sharma and colleagues (2017) classify why they fail as primary resistance (never works), adaptive resistance (the tumor responds to the T cells by raising its defenses) and acquired resistance (works, then stops). Oncolytic viruses address the first kind head on by bringing T cells in, and their link to the second kind is a tricky one: interferon-γ from the T cells they attract raises PD-L1 on tumor cells (Garcia-Diaz et al. 2017). That up-regulation is a brake, but it’s also exactly what a PD-1 or PD-L1 antibody releases. So the two treatments fit together in a mechanistic way. Virus brings in the T cells and ensures a strong interferon environment. The antibody keeps the interferon-induced brake from stopping the response.

The preclinical case is strong. NDV in a melanoma model rendered tumors sensitive to CTLA-4 blockade, including in distant tumors that weren’t injected (Zamarin et al. 2014). Viral infection of tumors broadened the neoantigen response and overcame PD-1 resistance (Woller et al. 2015). Measles virus combined with anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-L1 improved control in mouse models (Engeland et al. 2014), and with anti-PD-1 in glioblastoma models (Hardcastle et al. 2017). Neoadjuvant Maraba virus before surgery improved the response to checkpoint therapy in mouse breast cancer (Bourgeois-Daigneault et al. 2018). The clinical case is more mixed: strong early-phase results with T-VEC and pembrolizumab (Ribas et al. 2017), a randomized phase 2 gain with ipilimumab (Chesney et al. 2018), and then the negative phase 3 result (Chesney et al. 2023). Reviews by Bommareddy and colleagues (2018) and Sivanandam and colleagues (2019) lay out the rationale and the clinical record. RP1 plus nivolumab in anti-PD-1-refractory melanoma, the basis of the 2026 approval, is the first combination of an oncolytic virus and a checkpoint inhibitor to receive regulatory approval in the United States.

9.3 Pairing with cell therapies

CAR T cells, T cells engineered to recognize a tumor surface protein, have transformed treatment of some blood cancers but have done poorly in solid tumors, in part because of a hostile microenvironment and antigen heterogeneity. Oncolytic viruses are a natural partner, and Guedan and Alemany (2018) summarize the approaches. An adenovirus engineered to release the chemokine RANTES and IL-15 improved CAR T cell trafficking and survival in a neuroblastoma model (Nishio et al. 2014). A virus that made a PD-L1-blocking mini-antibody boosted CAR T cells in a solid tumor model (Tanoue et al. 2017). And an adenovirus that made a bispecific engager directed at a second antigen allowed CAR T cells to target tumor cells that lacked the CAR’s own target (Wing et al. 2018). These are preclinical results so far, but the logic is neat: the virus remodels the tumor and broadens the target set, and the T cells do the killing.

9.4 Other pairings

Radiotherapy and some chemotherapies also cause immunogenic cell death, and combining them with viruses has been explored, though scheduling matters, because killing the T cells you just recruited would be counterproductive (see the review by Wang and colleagues 2025). Routes of delivery matter too. Injecting directly into a tumor concentrates the virus where it’s needed, but only reaches accessible tumors, and the argument for systemic delivery, which could reach metastases, is balanced by the barriers described in the next section.

10. The immune system fights back: friend and foe

It would be convenient if the immune response to an oncolytic virus were a single, unambiguous good. It isn’t. The same machinery that attacks the tumor also attacks the virus, and Marelli and colleagues (2018) rightly called it a double-edged sword. Lemos de Matos, Franco and McFadden (2020) offer a more optimistic framing of the pair as a dynamic duo, and the truth lies between them.

Antibodies. Many adults already carry neutralizing antibodies against common viruses such as adenovirus, HSV, measles and vaccinia, whether from infection or vaccination. Those antibodies can neutralize a virus injected into the bloodstream before it reaches the tumor. Injection directly into a tumor or the bladder avoids much of the problem, and treatment itself raises antibody levels, which makes repeated intravenous dosing hard. Some groups have tried hiding the virus inside carrier cells. Reovirus carried inside human dendritic cells was protected from neutralization (Ilett et al. 2011), and cell-based carriers carrying virus delivered it to tumors in the face of antiviral immunity in mouse models (Power et al. 2007).

Innate effector cells. As described earlier, NK cells and macrophages can eliminate virus-infected tumor cells before the virus has spread and made its mark, and in glioma models blocking this response improved viral therapy (Alvarez-Breckenridge et al. 2012; Fulci et al. 2007). The same cells that cause trouble early on contribute to the later immune response. Their effect depends on timing and dose, and it’s one reason that some groups are testing very early, very short suppression of the innate response, a strategy that still has to be tested in people.

T cells against the virus. Cytotoxic T cells that recognize viral peptides kill infected tumor cells, which limits viral spread, but it’s also an anticancer effect, since each killed cell releases tumor antigen in an inflammatory setting. Pre-existing immunity to a virus, depending on the setting, can sometimes enhance therapeutic effect in mouse models (Ricca et al. 2018), probably because memory T cells respond rapidly and bring inflammatory help to the tumor. The balance seems to vary with the virus, the tumor and the route of delivery.

Less-studied players. Neutrophils flood into infected tumors and can both help and hurt. Complement attacks enveloped viruses in the blood. Antibodies against tumor antigens can form during the response and may contribute to tumor control, although this has been looked at much less than the T cell response. Gamma-delta T cells and NKT cells, which respond to stress and lipid signals rather than to peptides, are also activated by infection, but their role in oncolytic virus therapy is still poorly mapped. This is an honest area of ignorance.

10.1 Evolution inside the patient

The evolutionary story doesn’t end with the design of the virus. Once a virus and a tumor are put together, both go on evolving.

On the virus side, RNA viruses such as VSV, measles, poliovirus and reovirus mutate quickly because their polymerases make errors and don’t proofread. They exist as clouds of related variants, called quasispecies, from which selection can pick the best fit to a new environment (Domingo and Holland 1997). That makes them adaptable, and it makes them a risk if an attenuating change can revert. This is part of why PVSRIPO uses a replaced IRES rather than the point mutations of the original vaccine strain. Researchers have turned the same property into a tool: by passaging viruses repeatedly in tumor cells, they have selected reovirus, paramyxovirus, enterovirus and rhabdovirus variants with better safety, selectivity or spread, a method called directed evolution (Zainutdinov et al. 2019). DNA viruses such as HSV, adenovirus and vaccinia are far more stable, which is part of their appeal for engineering.

On the tumor side, tumors are genetically heterogeneous and evolve in a branching pattern, with different regions carrying different mutations (Gerlinger et al. 2012). A population like that is likely to contain cells that happen to resist a virus and then to take over if the virus clears the rest. Systematic reviews and recent studies show that resistance can arise from many sources: restored or enhanced interferon signaling, loss of the viral entry receptor, epigenetic silencing of viral promoters, a dense matrix that blocks the virus, hypoxia, and stromal cells that clear the virus (Xu et al. 2025). A 2026 preprint on glioblastoma cells that were made resistant to Sindbis virus or parvovirus reported that resistance tracked with impaired viral replication, with increased antiviral gene expression and dependence on type I interferon in some lines, and that one resistant line was also resistant to several other viruses (Deconinck et al. 2026, not yet peer reviewed). In other words, a tumor that finds a way to resist one virus may resist many, which argues for combining strategies.

Mathematical models offer a way of thinking about this. Wodarz (2001) showed that whether a virus can control a tumor depends on a balance among the replication rate of the virus, the death rate of infected cells and the growth rate of the tumor, and that the immune response can tilt that balance in either direction. Wodarz and Komarova (2009) extended this into models that can be tested against experimental data. These are simplifications, but they carry a useful message: a virus that kills too fast burns out before it spreads, and one that kills too slowly is outrun by the tumor.

There’s also a longer-term evolutionary pressure on the tumor from the immune response the virus creates. If oncolytic therapy succeeds in generating tumor-specific T cells, the surviving tumor cells that escape, for instance by losing MHC class I or the antigen itself, will be the ones that grow back. That is classic immunoediting (Schreiber et al. 2011), and it’s a strong argument for making the T cell response as broad as possible, because a tumor can lose one antigen far more easily than twenty. Epitope spreading is the field’s main protection against that outcome.

11. What we still don’t know

Several honest problems remain.

Biomarkers. There’s no reliable test to tell which patients will respond. Zainutdinov and colleagues (2019) noted that no biomarker was known to predict response, and that remains largely true. Candidates include pre-existing T cell infiltration, interferon pathway status of the tumor, the presence of the viral entry receptor, and baseline antibody levels, but none is validated.

Durability and reach. Responses can be impressive and sometimes long-lasting, but most patients don’t respond, and even among responders injected lesions respond better than uninjected ones. Whether a locally administered virus can reliably generate immunity strong enough to clear distant disease in more than a minority of patients is still being tested.

Trial design. Several approvals and applications have rested on single-arm trials, and the two rejections of RP1 before its approval turned on exactly that issue, whether such data can show that a treatment works. The phase 3 failures of Pexa-Vec in liver cancer and of T-VEC plus pembrolizumab in melanoma show the risk of relying on early response rates. Randomized confirmatory trials will matter a lot over the next few years.

Dose, schedule and sequence. How much virus, how often, before or after surgery, and in what order relative to checkpoint inhibitors, are all open questions. Timing relative to the innate and adaptive antiviral responses may determine whether a given dose helps or hurts.

Safety. Most oncolytic viruses have been well tolerated, with flu-like symptoms and injection-site reactions being the most common side effects. HSV can reactivate, shed and, rarely, be passed to close contacts, which is why precautions are given to patients and caregivers, and immunocompromised patients need special care. Long-term safety in children and in people with a long life expectancy remains less well known.

Mechanism in people. Most of the detailed mechanisms described in this essay come from mouse models, and mouse tumors are not human tumors. Human biopsy data (Kaufman et al. 2010; Ribas et al. 2017; Samson et al. 2018; Lang et al. 2018) support the main outline, but how much of the benefit in any given patient is direct killing, innate activation, epitope spreading or microenvironment change is not known.

Putting it together

If you wanted the whole essay in a few sentences, it would go like this. Cancer cells evolve under selection to grow and to hide, and in doing so they often give up defenses, especially the interferon system and growth-control pathways that viruses also depend on, that normal cells keep. Viruses that evolved to defeat those defenses can be tamed by deleting the parts that fight them, so that they thrive in tumors and falter in healthy tissue. Inside the tumor, infection triggers sensors that are hundreds of millions of years older than the adaptive immune system, producing interferon and inflammation, and the infected cells die in ways that spill out both tumor antigens and danger signals. Dendritic cells take up that material, mature, and train T cells that recognize the virus and, crucially, the tumor. The microenvironment, which was suppressing immunity, is rebuilt into one that favors it. The tumor, in effect, has been turned from something the immune system ignores into something it targets. That outcome is real but incomplete: the same immune system also clears the virus, tumors evolve resistance, and the clinical benefit so far is meaningful for a minority of patients and unproven for most. The fact that a handful of different viruses have now reached approval, most recently RP1 in 2026, shows the idea has legs, and the next few years of randomized trials will say how far.
