title: What makes glioblastoma difficult to treat?
summary: Glioblastoma combines invasive growth, cellular diversity, and a tumor microenvironment that can limit therapy.
body:
Introduction

Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults and one of the most lethal solid cancers. US registry data (CBTRUS, 2014–2018) recorded about 61,700 cases over five years, a median age at diagnosis of 65, and an age-adjusted incidence of 3.23 per 100,000 [1]. Population-level analyses covering 2001–2017 report a five-year relative survival of roughly 6.8% and a median overall survival of about eight months across all patients, rising to 12–14 months in those who receive surgery plus combined chemoradiation; five-year survival in patients older than 65 is about 2.7% [2].

Since the 2021 WHO classification of CNS tumors (WHO CNS5), GBM is defined as a diffuse astrocytic glioma that is IDH-wildtype and H3-wildtype and that shows microvascular proliferation or necrosis, or carries at least one of three molecular hallmarks: TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or combined gain of chromosome 7 and loss of chromosome 10 (+7/−10) [3]. Tumors that were formerly called “IDH-mutant glioblastoma” are now classified as astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 4 [3]. This matters for reading the literature: this review concerns IDH-wildtype disease, but older trials were run under earlier definitions.

Reviews of the field converge on a set of interacting reasons why durable disease control remains uncommon: limited and heterogeneous drug delivery across the blood–brain barrier, enhanced DNA repair capacity, persistence of stem-like tumor cells, profound immunosuppression within the tumor microenvironment, and extensive intratumoral heterogeneity with ongoing clonal evolution [4,5]. The sections below take each in turn, together with the clinical-trial evidence that illustrates it. Where a finding rests on a single preclinical study, a retrospective analysis or a non-randomized trial, that is stated, because in GBM the gap between promising early data and randomized benefit has been the rule rather than the exception.

1. The clinical benchmark: what current therapy achieves

Standard care for newly diagnosed GBM is maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (TMZ). The pivotal EORTC-NCIC trial randomized 573 patients at 85 centers to radiotherapy alone or radiotherapy plus daily TMZ followed by up to six adjuvant cycles. Median overall survival was 14.6 months with combined therapy versus 12.1 months with radiotherapy alone (hazard ratio for death 0.63), and two-year survival was 26.5% versus 10.4% [6]. Median progression-free survival was 6.9 versus 5.0 months. The benefit persisted through five-year follow-up, when roughly 10% of patients in the combination arm were alive [8,9]. The effect is real, but it amounts to a median gain of about 2.5 months.

The companion study showed that the benefit is concentrated in a molecularly defined subgroup. The DNA-repair enzyme MGMT removes the methyl adducts that TMZ places on DNA, and silencing of the MGMT promoter by methylation, present in roughly 45% of assessable tumors, predicts benefit. Among patients with methylated promoters, median survival was 21.7 months with TMZ plus radiotherapy versus 15.3 months with radiotherapy alone; in unmethylated tumors the difference was not significant [7]. In other words, for the majority of patients, the one cytotoxic drug that improved survival in a phase III trial adds little.

The only other modality shown to extend survival in newly diagnosed GBM in a phase III trial is Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields), low-intensity alternating electric fields delivered through scalp arrays. In EF-14, 695 patients who had completed chemoradiation were randomized 2:1 to maintenance TMZ with or without TTFields. Median progression-free survival was 6.7 versus 4.0 months and median overall survival 20.9 versus 16.0 months (hazard ratio 0.63 for both); survival at two years was 43% versus 31%, and at five years 13% versus 5% [9]. The trial was open-label, and the benefit in MGMT-unmethylated tumors was smaller (16.9 versus 14.7 months) [9]. A small randomized phase II trial (66 patients) of TTFields given concurrently with radiotherapy and TMZ reported no statistically significant difference in progression-free or overall survival [10].

Recurrence is nearly universal after standard therapy [66]. Options at recurrence include re-operation, re-irradiation, nitrosoureas such as lomustine, TMZ rechallenge, and bevacizumab [52]. Outcomes are poor: in the bevacizumab control arm of the CheckMate 143 randomized trial, median overall survival was 10.0 months [12], and in the external control population of the DCVax-L trial, median survival from relapse was 7.8 months [54].

2. Diffuse infiltration: by diagnosis, the tumor has usually left the surgical field

Surgery cannot cure GBM because the tumor is not a discrete mass. In a series of 20 patients whose contrast-enhancing tumor was completely resected and who then received radiotherapy and TMZ, 17 recurred only at the resection margin, 2 only at a distant site and 1 at both, so 85% of recurrences involved the margin [14]. An earlier CT-based analysis found that 78% of unifocal tumors recurred within 2.0 cm of the original enhancing margin and 56% within 1.0 cm [13]. A more recent study summarizes that about 80% of gliomas fail within 2 cm of the resection cavity despite aggressive local treatment, and in a temporal-lobe cohort 74% of first recurrences were locoregional, 26% were distant, and 53% involved neural pathways, meaning white matter tracts [15]. Distant or non-local recurrence is common enough to matter: in a 5-ALA-guided surgery cohort of 77 patients, 34.5% of first recurrences were non-local, and a larger preoperative enhancing volume was associated with a higher non-local rate [16].

Two practical consequences follow. First, the microscopic infiltrate lies in brain that looks normal or only edematous on standard imaging; FLAIR hyperintensity characterizes early infiltration, but the extent of true tumor spread is uncertain, so radiotherapy protocols use generous uniform margins [15]. Second, simply escalating local treatment does not work: older studies of hyperfractionated dose escalation showed no improvement in control or survival, and doses up to 90 Gy produced unacceptable radiation necrosis [15].

The invasion itself is an active biological program. Single glioma cells co-opt existing blood vessels to travel through the parenchyma [11], tumor spread along white matter tracts is well documented clinically [15], and in astrocytomas, ultra-long membrane protrusions called tumor microtubes serve as routes for brain invasion (Section 7) [30]. Because the invading cells sit largely behind an intact blood–brain barrier, infiltration and drug delivery are linked problems, which brings us to the next section.

3. The blood–brain and blood–tumor barriers

The blood–brain barrier (BBB) is a non-fenestrated barrier built from specialized capillary endothelial cells joined by multi-protein tight junctions (claudins, occludin, zonula occludens proteins), supported by pericytes and astrocytic endfeet [5,11]. It excludes most chemotherapeutic and biologic agents.

In GBM the barrier is not uniformly intact. It is heterogeneously disrupted to form a “blood–tumor barrier,” characterized by abnormal pericyte distribution, reduced tight junctions, loss of astrocytic endfeet and increased permeability to circulating immune cells; this produces regional niches of variable permeability to blood, oxygen, nutrients and drugs [11]. Contrast enhancement on MRI marks where the barrier is leaky, but it is only part of the tumor: beyond it, essentially all GBM have a region of non-enhancing, T2/FLAIR-bright infiltrated brain in which the barrier is largely preserved. Sarkaria and colleagues have argued that limited and heterogeneous drug delivery across the BBB is a major reason for the lack of therapeutic progress, and that any effective regimen must address this non-enhancing, infiltrating tumor burden [17]. The extent to which the BBB limits efficacy in GBM has been debated, since the tumor core is leaky, and the evidence is strongest where it has been tested pharmacologically.

Active efflux is a second layer of protection. The ATP-binding cassette transporters P-glycoprotein (P-gp, ABCB1) and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP, ABCG2) pump substrate drugs from endothelial cells back into blood, and they work as a cooperative pair: inhibiting both is generally needed to raise brain penetration substantially [19]. In mouse models, combined deletion of Abcb1a/b and Abcg2, or co-administration of the dual inhibitor elacridar, increased brain penetration of TMZ by about 1.5-fold without altering plasma exposure, and improved TMZ efficacy against three independent intracranial tumor models [18]. For the kinase inhibitor dasatinib, active efflux limited efficacy against glioma in mice despite a leaky tumor core, and most human glioma xenograft lines tested expressed BCRP or P-gp themselves, creating a second, tumor-intrinsic efflux barrier [19]. Efflux transporters are also expressed in stem-like glioma cells. Clinically, however, attempts to modulate efflux pumps have largely been unsuccessful [11].

Delivery is necessary but not sufficient. TMZ is lipophilic, orally available and crosses the BBB [20], yet it extends median survival by only a few months and fails to help most MGMT-unmethylated tumors. The failure of many kinase inhibitors, immunotherapies and antibody-based agents therefore reflects delivery plus biology. Strategies under investigation to improve delivery include local administration (carmustine wafers are used locally because of poor BBB penetration of carmustine [20]), convection-enhanced and focused-ultrasound-mediated delivery, nanocarriers, and pharmacologic opening of the barrier, for example BMX inhibition with ibrutinib, which in preclinical work selectively increased blood–tumor barrier permeability [11]. For cell therapies and immune effectors, barrier-associated trafficking limits are an additional obstacle, one reason that recent CAR-T trials moved to intraventricular and intrathecal delivery (Section 9).

4. Heterogeneity, plasticity, and glioblastoma stem cells

4.1 Cellular states

Bulk transcriptional profiling divided GBM into proneural, classical and mesenchymal subtypes, which describes differences between patients. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that the more fundamental problem is variation within each tumor. Neftel and colleagues combined single-cell sequencing of 28 tumors with bulk analysis of 401 TCGA specimens, functional work and lineage tracing, and found that malignant cells exist in four main states that recapitulate neural cell types: neural-progenitor-like (NPC-like), oligodendrocyte-progenitor-like (OPC-like), astrocyte-like (AC-like) and mesenchymal-like (MES-like). The cells are plastic, can transition between states, and the proportion of each state in a given tumor is shaped by genetics (amplification of CDK4, EGFR and PDGFRA and mutation of NF1 each favor a particular state) and by the microenvironment [21]. Each tumor has a dominant state, with the mesenchymal and classical subtypes enriched for MES-like and AC-like cells and the proneural subtype enriched for OPC-like and NPC-like cells [23].

The microenvironment directly drives these transitions. In mouse models and glioma-sphere systems, macrophages induced a shift of tumor cells toward the MES-like state [22]. Spatial transcriptomic work shows that these states are organized in space: MES-like territories form distinct regions, AC-like and OPC-like cells co-localize, and the tumor’s pattern is closely shaped by its vasculature [24]. Therapy also acts on this landscape. In patient-derived lines tracked with proneural and mesenchymal fluorescent reporters, a hybrid population expressing both identities was resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy and was enriched by treatment; interfering with the machinery sustaining this hybrid state suppressed plasticity and increased sensitivity in preclinical models [23].

Plasticity has a direct clinical correlate in antigen escape. EGFRvIII, a constitutively active deletion variant, is found in roughly 23–33% of GBM, and EGFR expression varies greatly from cell to cell within a tumor. In the phase III ACT IV trial, EGFRvIII expression was lost at recurrence in 57–59% of tumors regardless of whether patients had received the EGFRvIII vaccine or control, showing that the loss is part of natural tumor evolution rather than a consequence of immune pressure.

4.2 Stem-like cells and niches

The cancer stem cell concept entered neuro-oncology when two groups isolated brain tumor stem cells from human gliomas as self-renewing spheres that produced differentiated progeny and reproduced the tumor on transplantation [26]. In 2006, Bao and colleagues reported that CD133-expressing glioma cells were enriched after irradiation, survived radiation better, activated the DNA damage checkpoint more strongly and repaired radiation-induced breaks more effectively than CD133-negative cells; a Chk1/Chk2 inhibitor reversed the radioresistance [25]. A commentary on the study noted that both populations sustained the same initial damage but that repair occurred 4–9 times faster in CD133+ cells [25]. Conventional treatment of high-grade glioma in patients has also been associated with expansion of the CD133+ population, suggesting that these cells preferentially survive therapy [26].

The picture has been refined since. Not all CD133+ cells are radioresistant [26], and one later comparison found that CD133+ tumor stem-like cell lines were in vitro more radiosensitive than established glioma lines, with reduced repair of double-strand breaks and a missing intra-S checkpoint [27]. Together with the single-cell work, this suggests that stemness behaves less like a fixed cell identity and more like a plastic, context-dependent state that can be adopted by cells across the NPC-like/OPC-like compartments [21]; stem-like cells reside in perivascular and hypoxic niches that actively maintain them. The therapeutic point is robust even though the biology is contested: a tumor containing a self-renewing, repair-proficient, drug-effluxing subpopulation will regrow after treatments that kill the bulk.

4.3 Clonal evolution under treatment

Longitudinal sequencing has clarified what happens between diagnosis and recurrence. The GLASS consortium analyzed paired initial and recurrent tumors from 222 patients with diffuse glioma. Driver alterations present at diagnosis were retained at recurrence, and there was little evidence of recurrence-specific driver alterations; alkylating-agent treatment produced a hypermutator phenotype at varying rates across glioma types; and the authors concluded that the strongest selective pressures act early in glioma development and that current therapies shape evolution in a largely stochastic manner [28]. A larger follow-up integrating transcriptomic and genomic data (Varn et al., 2022) found that IDH-wildtype tumors were more invasive at recurrence and upregulated neuronal signaling programs, that recurrences clustered into neuronal, mesenchymal and proliferative phenotypes, and that hypermutation together with CDKN2A deletion was associated with a more proliferative, stem-like state at recurrence and with worse survival [29]. The two reports differ on the prognostic role of hypermutation (the 2019 analysis reported no survival difference), so this remains an active question.

The broad message supported by both is that recurrent GBM is not usually a genetically novel tumor. The same drivers persist, so resistance appears to rest heavily on pre-existing heterogeneity and non-genetic plasticity, which is one explanation (an interpretation, not a proven mechanism) for why serial targeted therapies against single drivers have failed (Section 9).

5. DNA repair and resistance to temozolomide and radiation

TMZ methylates DNA, producing damage that leads to cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis [20]. Resistance mechanisms catalogued in current reviews include enhanced DNA repair (most prominently MGMT), disrupted apoptosis, redundancy among survival pathways, altered drug metabolism, tolerance to oxidative stress, efflux, and stem-cell-mediated plasticity [20]; more recently described mechanisms include exosomal transfer of non-coding RNAs and metabolic reprogramming [5]. The decisive clinical marker remains MGMT promoter methylation: it is the strongest predictor of outcome and of benefit from TMZ in the EORTC-NCIC trial [6–8]. MGMT-unmethylated GBM, therefore, represents the largest group of patients with essentially no effective systemic therapy, and it is where most immunotherapy trials have been run (Section 9).

Radioresistance has overlapping roots. Bao’s work identified preferential checkpoint activation and rapid repair in stem-like cells [25]; later studies have implicated enhanced non-homologous end joining (for example through AATF) and rapid transcriptional reorganization during the adaptive response to radiation. Hypoxia and the tumor microenvironment contribute independently (Section 6), and tumor-cell networks protect connected cells from radiation (Section 7) [30]. Because TMZ and radiation are both DNA-damaging, and because treatment itself reshapes the surviving population, with hypermutation after alkylating therapy a frequent finding at recurrence [28,29], resistance to the standard regimen is built from several layers at once, none of which has so far been reliably drugged.

6. Hypoxia, necrosis and the vascular niche

Pseudopalisading necrosis (hypercellular zones surrounding necrotic foci) and microvascular proliferation are the histopathologic hallmarks of GBM [35]. They reflect a tumor that outgrows its disorganized blood supply and develops hypoxic regions, defined in the radiobiology literature as oxygen partial pressure below roughly 10 mmHg [38]. Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1α, a transcription factor that regulates on the order of 60 genes involved in glycolysis, angiogenesis, invasion and epithelial–mesenchymal-like transition [35]. In GBM, HIF-1 activity has been linked to angiogenesis, immunosuppression, metabolic reprogramming, invasion and stem-like phenotypes, and HIF-1 inhibitors have been studied as a result. HIF-1α and HIF-2α promote expansion of cancer stem cells and recruit macrophages [36], and abnormal vessels and pseudopalisading regions have been proposed to shelter stem-like cells from therapeutic agents [35].

Hypoxia therefore feeds several resistance mechanisms simultaneously. It is a main microenvironmental factor behind radioresistance, and a body of work has examined HIF signaling and stem-like cells as the molecular links [38]. It is also immunosuppressive: hypoxia reduces interferon-γ production by CD8+ T cells after T-cell-receptor stimulation and attenuates NK-cell cytotoxicity [37]. Spatial analyses place the tumor core, where hypoxia is greatest, as a niche enriched for MES-like tumor cells, monocyte-derived macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells, with exhausted T cells [41]. And the abnormal vasculature itself generates niches of variable permeability to oxygen and drugs [11]. Anti-angiogenic therapy, the most direct attempt to exploit this biology, has been useful only in a subset of patients [35]; in a trial of bevacizumab with irinotecan, hypoxia-induced carbonic anhydrase 9 (CA9) and HIF-2α were significant predictors of treatment effectiveness and survival [35].

7. Tumor networks and integration into neural circuits

Two lines of work, both from the past decade, show that GBM cells are not merely a mass of proliferating cells but a connected, activity-responsive system.

Tumor microtubes. In 2015, Osswald and colleagues showed that many astrocytoma cells extend ultra-long membrane protrusions, termed tumor microtubes, which serve as routes for brain invasion and proliferation and connect cells over long distances. The resulting network allows multicellular communication through microtube-associated gap junctions (connexin 43), and GAP-43 is important for microtube formation. When the network was damaged, microtubes were used for repair. Microtube-connected astrocytoma cells, but not unconnected cells, were protected from cell death caused by radiotherapy; in patient samples, more interconnected tumors were more malignant and resistant, whereas oligodendroglial tumors lacked the mechanism; and blocking the pathway in mice produced smaller tumors with fewer connections that were highly radiosensitive [30]. Subsequent work reported that microtubes also convey resistance to surgical lesions and to chemotherapy, and that the gap-junction inhibitor MFA reduced microtube length and, in a brain-slice model, increased the effect of TMZ [31].

Neuron–glioma synapses. In 2019, two Nature papers established that high-grade glioma progression is regulated by neuronal activity not only through secreted growth factors but through true synapses. Neurons form AMPA-receptor-dependent glutamatergic synapses onto glioma cells; depolarization of glioma membranes by optogenetics promotes proliferation; and genetic or pharmacologic blockade of this electrochemical signaling inhibits xenograft growth and extends survival in mice [32,33]. Gliomas also increase neuronal excitability, creating a positive feedback loop supported by intraoperative electrocorticography in patients, which showed increased cortical excitability in glioma-infiltrated cortex [32]. Glioma-specific perturbation of AMPA receptors, or chronic inhibition with the AMPA-receptor antagonist perampanel, reduced invasion and proliferation in mice [33]. Recurrent IDH-wildtype tumors up-regulate neuronal signaling programs [29], and later studies have tied neuronal activity and glioma–neuron circuit remodeling to regional immunosuppression and checkpoint-blockade resistance in preclinical models [34].

The interpretation that follows is a reasoned inference rather than an established fact: because GBM is functionally integrated with normal brain circuitry and relies on pathways (gap junctions, glutamate receptors) that normal brain cells also use, targeting these mechanisms may have a narrow therapeutic window. To date, the evidence for both microtubes and synapses is preclinical, and neither has been tested in a randomized phase III trial.

8. An immunologically “cold,” myeloid-dominated microenvironment

GBM is frequently described as an immunologically cold tumor. Its low immunogenicity is characterized by low T-cell infiltration, a paucity of dendritic cells, low tumor mutational burden, limited MHC-I expression, an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and the lack of conventional draining lymph nodes [39]. A relatively moderate mutational burden compared with highly immunogenic cancers limits the neoantigens available to activate tumor-specific T cells, and GBM cells actively down-regulate MHC molecules [43]. The brain was once considered immune-privileged, and while that view has been revised, blood–brain barrier-associated trafficking limitations still affect how effector cells reach the tumor [42,43].

The microenvironment is dominated by myeloid cells. Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are the most abundant non-malignant cells and comprise tissue-resident microglia (of yolk-sac origin) and bone marrow-derived monocytes [40,42]. Estimates of their share depend on species and method: human studies are commonly cited as 30–50% of tumor mass [69], other reviews give 25–40% of tumor cellularity or “up to one-third” [44], and TAMs are reported to account for more than 80% of intratumoral immune cells [41]. These cells are not effective antigen presenters: glioma-associated microglia show reduced co-stimulatory molecules and impaired T-cell activation [69], and TAMs adopt tumor-supportive phenotypes with STAT3 activation, immunoregulatory cytokine secretion and impaired antigen presentation [44]. Monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells suppress T-cell proliferation through arginase-1 and nitric oxide, and regulatory T cells, neutrophils and glioma-derived extracellular vesicles contribute to the suppressive niche [42]. Effector lymphocytes, in contrast, are scarce, clonally restricted and transcriptionally exhausted [44]. TAMs are also reported to restrict T-cell infiltration spatially and to promote exhaustion [41]. Glioma cells add direct checkpoint engagement through PD-L1 and “don’t-eat-me” signaling through CD47–SIRPα on macrophages and microglia, where preclinical studies report that disrupting CD47–SIRPα signaling enhances tumor-cell clearance [42]. The immune landscape also changes across space and time, from primary to recurrent disease, and recurrent GBM is again dominated by TAMs [40,41].

This architecture explains why immunotherapies that work in immunogenic, T-cell-rich tumors have not transferred easily to GBM, a theme developed in the next section.

9. What the clinical trials have taught us

The biology above is best understood alongside the trials that tested it. Most failed, and the pattern of failure is informative.

9.1 Anti-angiogenic therapy: progression-free survival without survival

Bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody against VEGF-A, was approved for recurrent GBM on the basis of two phase II studies showing a progression-free survival benefit [11]. Two large placebo-controlled phase III trials then tested it upfront with chemoradiation. In RTOG 0825 (637 patients), median overall survival was 15.7 months with bevacizumab versus 16.1 months with placebo (hazard ratio 1.13), while median progression-free survival was 10.7 versus 7.3 months (hazard ratio 0.79); no subgroup with a survival benefit could be identified, and toxicity (hypertension, bleeding, thromboembolism, gastrointestinal perforation) was higher [45]. AVAglio (921 patients) found a similar split: progression-free survival 10.6 versus 6.2 months, but no overall survival benefit (two-year survival 33.9% versus 30.1%, P = 0.24), and more grade 3 or higher adverse events (66.8% versus 51.3%) [46]. The trials diverged on quality of life, which improved in AVAglio but not in RTOG 0825, and crossover to bevacizumab at progression may have obscured a survival effect [46]. A retrospective, exploratory analysis of AVAglio suggested that patients with IDH1-wildtype proneural tumors may derive a survival benefit, but this needs validation in an independent dataset [47].

The lesson is that delaying radiographic progression is not the same as extending life. One plausible reading (an interpretation) is that anti-VEGF therapy normalizes enhancement and permeability without eliminating the infiltrating, vessel-co-opting cells described above [11].

9.2 Targeted therapy: pathway redundancy and heterogeneity

The frequency of RTK/PI3K pathway alterations made GBM a natural candidate for targeted therapy. A 2017 review concluded that, although occasional responses were documented, no targeted therapy had been formally validated as effective in clinical trials [50]. EGFR is altered in roughly 60% of GBM, yet erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and lapatinib showed no efficacy alone or in combination [51]. An early single-institution phase II study of erlotinib with TMZ reported median survival of 19.3 months versus 14.1 months in historical controls, but subsequent trials were uniformly disappointing, and single-agent mTOR inhibitors also failed. Contributing explanations include weak sensitivity of EGFRvIII-driven tumors to first-generation EGFR inhibitors in preclinical models, redundant and compensatory signaling, and strong cellular plasticity that challenges the assumption that these alterations are obligate drivers [50,51]. This review does not cover newer agents tested in molecularly selected subgroups, which should be checked in a current source.

9.3 Immune checkpoint blockade

Checkpoint inhibitors transformed other cancers, so the PD-1 antibody nivolumab was tested in three phase III trials. In CheckMate 143 (369 randomized patients with recurrent GBM), median overall survival was 9.8 months with nivolumab versus 10.0 months with bevacizumab (hazard ratio 1.04; 12-month survival 42% in both arms), and the objective response rate was 7.8% versus 23.1% [12]. In CheckMate 498, nivolumab plus radiotherapy did not improve overall survival compared with TMZ plus radiotherapy in newly diagnosed MGMT-unmethylated GBM [48]. In CheckMate 548, nivolumab added to chemoradiation in MGMT-methylated or indeterminate GBM did not improve progression-free survival (10.6 versus 10.3 months; hazard ratio 1.06) or overall survival, and grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were more frequent (52.4% versus 33.6%) [49]. CheckMate 548 had been launched partly on the strength of an exploratory subgroup in CheckMate 143 (methylated MGMT, no baseline corticosteroids; 16.95 versus 10.12 months), a signal that did not hold up [49].

The immunology in Section 8 predicts this outcome: low neoantigen load, scarce and exhausted T cells, and a myeloid-dominated, hypoxic niche leave little for a checkpoint inhibitor to release [39,43].

9.4 Vaccines, dendritic cells and cell therapy

Rindopepimut targets EGFRvIII. In single-arm studies, patients with resected EGFRvIII-positive disease survived 20–22 months, compared with roughly 16 months for matched contemporary controls [52]. The randomized, double-blind phase III ACT IV trial (745 patients) found no benefit: median overall survival was 20.4 months with the vaccine and 21.1 months with control (hazard ratio 0.99), despite a robust antibody response [52]. The control arm matched the single-arm results, which indicates that the earlier comparisons with historical controls were inflated by selection of well-resected patients with minimal residual disease. As described in Section 4.1, EGFRvIII was lost at recurrence in 57–59% of patients in both arms [52,55].

DCVax-L, an autologous tumor-lysate-loaded dendritic cell vaccine, was evaluated in a phase 3 trial that enrolled 331 patients (232 to DCVax-L, 99 to placebo). The reported comparison was against contemporaneous matched external controls drawn from other trials: median overall survival was 19.3 versus 16.5 months in newly diagnosed GBM (hazard ratio 0.80), with 13.0% versus 5.7% alive at 60 months, and 13.2 versus 7.8 months from relapse in recurrent GBM [54]. Because patients whose tumors recurred were offered the vaccine [54] and the principal comparison was non-randomized, the trial’s authors characterized it as an association, and statisticians have called for explicit statements of the estimand and assumptions, and for access to the code and external data, before external-control analyses are interpreted as causal [55].

CAR-T cells produced some of the most striking early radiographic responses reported in GBM. In 2024, three first-in-human studies were reported. At Massachusetts General Hospital, three patients with recurrent GBM received intraventricular CARv3-TEAM-E T cells (an EGFRvIII-directed CAR plus a secreted T-cell-engaging antibody molecule against wild-type EGFR); there were no adverse events above grade 3 or dose-limiting toxicities, and tumors regressed within days, but responses were transient in two of the three patients [56]. At the University of Pennsylvania, six patients with recurrent EGFR-amplified GBM received intrathecal bivalent CAR-T cells directed at an EGFR epitope and IL13Rα2, a design chosen to address antigen heterogeneity, and all six had tumor reduction within two days [57]. City of Hope reported locoregional delivery of IL13Rα2-directed CAR-T cells in a phase 1 trial [58]. These studies were small and safety-focused, and part of the early regression may reflect inflammation after the surgery needed to place the delivery catheter. Mechanistically, failure of earlier intravenous EGFRvIII CAR-T therapy has been attributed to spatial heterogeneity, rapid down-regulation of EGFRvIII under immune pressure, and a myeloid-dominant, TGF-β-rich niche that drives T-cell exhaustion and limits persistence [59].

10. Why translation is so difficult: methodological obstacles

Beyond the biology, several features of the research enterprise slow progress.

Models. The translational gap between promising preclinical findings and proven clinical benefit remains substantial [60]. Established cell lines, patient-derived xenografts, syngeneic models and organoids each capture some features of GBM and miss others [61]; in one organoid-based study, a large part of the NPC-like and AC-like compartments was lost when cells were returned to 2D culture without the organoid microenvironment [73].

Response assessment. Pseudoprogression, transient radiographic worsening within about six months after chemoradiation that reflects an exaggerated treatment response, complicates the interpretation of early imaging [62]. Imaging also under-detects the non-enhancing infiltrative component (Section 2), and drugs that alter vascular permeability can change enhancement without changing tumor burden (Section 9.1), which weakens progression-free survival as a surrogate.

Trial design and controls. Single-arm trials against historical controls overestimated benefit (rindopepimut), exploratory subgroups generated hypotheses that failed to replicate (nivolumab in methylated, steroid-free patients), and external-control analyses remain contentious (DCVax-L) [49,52,55].

A moving target. Genetic drivers persist at recurrence, but the cellular state, invasiveness, proliferation and microenvironment change [28,29]. A biopsy taken at diagnosis may not represent the cells that regrow, and few trials are designed around recurrent-tissue analysis.

11. Where the field is directing its effort

Current reviews converge on a few directions, none yet proven in phase III: precision approaches that integrate molecular profiling, rational multimodal combinations, and better strategies for drug delivery and immune modulation [4]. More specifically:

  • Targeting plasticity. Lineage plasticity and cellular-state transitions are considered one of the most active areas, with preclinical evidence that suppressing hybrid proneural–mesenchymal states increases therapy sensitivity [23,60]. Recent preclinical work has also explored combined targeting of stem-like cells in different states [65].

  • Barrier-penetrant and locally delivered drugs. Designing agents that avoid efflux, using convection-enhanced or focused-ultrasound delivery, and engineering nanocarriers [44]. Clinical translation of efflux inhibition remains limited [11].

  • Disconnecting tumor networks and circuits. Gap-junction and GAP-43 targeting, and AMPA-receptor blockade, are supported by mouse data only [30,31,33].

  • Reprogramming the myeloid compartment. Because TAMs and MDSCs are thought to drive T-cell exhaustion, targeting them may be a prerequisite for effective checkpoint blockade or CAR-T therapy [74].

  • Antigen-diverse cell therapy. Multi-antigen and bispecific-engaging CAR-T cells delivered into the ventricles or cerebrospinal fluid, with the open questions of durability and persistence [56–59].

  • Physical modalities. TTFields is the one example of a physical modality with phase III survival data [9]; its earlier integration with chemoradiation has so far been tested only in a small randomized phase II trial [10].

Conclusion

No single feature makes glioblastoma difficult to treat. The established picture is of interlocking problems. The tumor infiltrates diffusely along white matter and vessels, so that by diagnosis cells lie beyond any surgical or radiation field and in regions where the blood–brain barrier is largely intact and efflux pumps limit drug entry. The cells are heterogeneous and plastic, cycling among neural-progenitor-, oligodendrocyte-progenitor-, astrocyte- and mesenchymal-like states under the influence of genetics and the microenvironment, and a stem-like, repair-proficient subpopulation survives treatment. Hypoxic niches, tumor-cell networks and neuron–glioma synapses add protective and growth-promoting layers. The immune system is largely excluded, exhausted or co-opted by a myeloid-dominated, immunosuppressive microenvironment. And under therapy the tumor evolves, keeping its drivers while shifting state and sometimes becoming hypermutated and more proliferative.

These factors link causally: hypoxia promotes stemness, radioresistance and immunosuppression together; infiltration places tumor behind the barrier; plasticity produces antigen escape. That is why single-mechanism interventions, whether kinase inhibitors, anti-angiogenics, checkpoint inhibitors or vaccines, have so often produced early signals that did not survive randomized testing. The modest gains that are established (temozolomide in MGMT-methylated tumors, and TTFields) are measured in months, and the most promising recent signals, locoregional cell therapies, remain early-phase. The open questions are how to deliver effective agents to infiltrating cells, how to address plasticity rather than a single state, and how to restore effective antitumor immunity in a tumor whose microenvironment is built to prevent it.

Scope and caveats. This review is based on peer-reviewed trial reports and recent review articles retrieved in November 2026. Estimates such as the share of myeloid cells in tumors vary between sources and methods, and several of the findings described here come from preclinical or early-phase studies. It is an educational overview and not medical advice; treatment decisions should be made with a qualified neuro-oncology team.

title: RNA sequencing: from reads to biological questions
summary: A practical overview of how RNA-seq can reveal gene-expression patterns and generate testable hypotheses.
body:
1. The big idea, in plain language

Every cell in your body carries essentially the same DNA, yet a neuron and a liver cell behave very differently. The difference is which genes are switched on. When a gene is active, the cell copies it into RNA, a working copy that directs the cell’s machinery. The full collection of RNA in a cell or tissue is its transcriptome.

RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) reads that collection. RNA is converted to DNA, cut into fragments, and passed through a sequencing machine. The machine outputs millions to billions of short text strings called reads, each a few dozen to a few hundred letters (A, C, G, T). Software works out which gene each read came from and counts them. A gene with many reads was highly active, and one with few reads was quiet. From those counts scientists can ask what separates a tumour from healthy tissue, how a drug alters a cell, or which genes turn on as an embryo develops.

The path from raw reads to a biological answer has many steps, and each involves choices that can change the conclusion. This essay follows that path.

2. Where RNA-seq came from

Before RNA-seq, gene activity was measured mostly with hybridization microarrays or Sanger sequencing of cDNA. In their 2009 review, Wang, Gerstein and Snyder described RNA-seq as offering single-base resolution of transcript boundaries, very low background, and the ability to work with less RNA than earlier approaches [1]. At that time Illumina, SOLiD and 454 platforms were being applied to RNA-seq, and RNA had to be fragmented into pieces of roughly 200–500 bp [1]. Mortazavi and colleagues’ 2008 paper on mapping and quantifying mammalian transcriptomes was one of the founding studies of the field [2].

A decade later, Stark, Grzelak and Hadfield described RNA-seq as indispensable for transcriptome-wide analysis of expression and splicing. They noted that variations now extend to single-cell, translation, RNA-structure and spatial measurements, and that Illumina short-read technology generated more than 95% of the RNA-seq data in the Short Read Archive [4].

3. Designing the experiment

Conesa and colleagues surveyed best practices for the whole workflow. Their central conclusion is that there is no single optimal pipeline for every application, so each scenario may need different methods [3]. Good design matters most, because no software can rescue a poorly designed experiment.

Biological replicates. A replicate is an independent sample, such as a different animal, patient or culture, not the same sample measured twice. Three replicates per condition is common but often too few. Schurch and colleagues sequenced yeast with 48 replicates per condition. They found that with three replicates, most tools recovered only a minority of the significant genes found with the full dataset. Detection of genes changing more than fourfold was much better, and the authors recommended at least six replicates, and at least twelve when small fold changes matter [5]. (A published erratum corrected part of that paper’s analysis [5].)

Sequencing depth. For standard differential-expression work, Stark and colleagues describe roughly 10–30 million reads per sample as typical. Rare transcripts, isoforms and fusion genes usually need more [4].

Controls against hidden bias. Samples should be spread across lanes and processing days so that biology is not confounded with batch. Spike-in controls such as the ERCC synthetic RNAs help calibrate measurements.

RNA quality. Labs check RNA integrity with instruments such as the Agilent Bioanalyzer or TapeStation, which report an RNA Integrity Number (RIN). Degraded material, such as formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue, needs specialised kits.

4. Preparing the library

Stark and colleagues summarise the standard bulk workflow as RNA extraction, enrichment of mRNA or depletion of ribosomal RNA, cDNA synthesis, adaptor-ligated library preparation and sequencing [4]. In more detail:

  1. Extract RNA (for example, TRIzol or column kits).

  2. Choose which RNA to read. Most RNA in a cell is ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which is rarely the target. Researchers either capture mRNA by its poly(A) tail, which suits intact RNA, or remove rRNA, which also keeps non-coding and bacterial RNA and tolerates degraded samples.

  3. Fragment and reverse-transcribe into complementary DNA (cDNA).

  4. Ligate adapters that bind the sequencer and carry sample barcodes so many samples can be pooled.

  5. Amplify by PCR, which introduces some bias.

  6. Optional features. Strand-specific protocols record which strand an RNA came from. Unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) tag each original molecule so PCR duplicates can be collapsed.

5. Sequencing platforms

5.1 Short-read platforms

Illumina dominates and uses sequencing-by-synthesis: fluorescently labelled bases are added to DNA clusters on a flow cell and imaged.

  • NovaSeq X / X Plus. Illumina’s specification sheet lists up to 16 terabases and up to 52 billion single reads per dual-flow-cell run on the X Plus, and up to 8 Tb and 26 billion single reads on the single-flow-cell NovaSeq X [31]. Flow cells come in 1.5B, 10B and 25B sizes [31]. Illumina’s own estimates are about 30, 200 and 520 transcriptomes per flow cell respectively for the three types [31].

  • NextSeq 1000/2000. A mid-throughput benchtop system. One core facility lists 100 million reads for a P1 flow cell and 400 million for a P2 [32].

Element Biosciences AVITI uses “avidity” chemistry. A published utility analysis reports about one billion polonies per flow cell and a 32.5% lower average RNA-quantification error rate than the NextSeq 550 [33]. A university core-facility comparison on 64 RNA-seq libraries found slightly higher quality scores on AVITI but a difference unlikely to require workflow changes [34]. Element has also launched a higher-throughput system called Vitari to compete with NovaSeq X, Ultima’s UG 100 and Complete Genomics’ DNBSeq-T7 [35].

Ultima Genomics UG100 and MGI/Complete Genomics DNBSEQ are further high-throughput options. A 2026 preprint benchmarking UG100 against NovaSeq in FFPE tissue reported highly comparable RNA results, including for lowly expressed genes [36]. Vendor-run comparisons (for example MGI’s) should be treated as marketing until independently replicated.

5.2 Long-read platforms

Short reads shatter transcripts, so it is hard to know which exons sit together in one molecule. Long reads can span a whole transcript.

  • PacBio Iso-Seq sequences full-length cDNA by single-molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing.

  • Oxford Nanopore (ONT) reads the change in electrical current as a nucleic-acid strand passes through a pore. It can sequence amplified cDNA, unamplified cDNA or native RNA (direct RNA sequencing) [29]. Read lengths reach about 15 kb for PacBio and over 30 kb for ONT, beyond the length of most transcripts [37].

  • Direct RNA sequencing reads the RNA itself, with no reverse transcription or amplification, so a single read can carry information on full-length structure, splicing, poly(A) tail features and base modifications [38].

5.3 Single-cell and spatial platforms

  • 10x Genomics Chromium is a droplet system. Its original paper described 3′ mRNA counting of tens of thousands of single cells per sample, with each cell barcoded and each molecule given a UMI [24]. Alternatives include Drop-seq [27] and plate-based full-length methods such as Smart-seq2.

  • 10x Visium (spatial). mRNA diffuses from tissue onto a slide carrying oligo-dT primers with UMIs and spatial barcodes, and the captured cDNA is pooled and sequenced [4]. A comparison with NanoString GeoMx notes that GeoMx is targeted, whereas Visium maps the whole transcriptome at relatively high spatial resolution [39].

  • Single-cell scale follows sequencer capacity. Illumina estimates that a 25B NovaSeq X flow cell could sequence about 2 million cells per run at 25,000 reads per cell [31].

6. From reads to counts

Conesa and colleagues list the main analysis steps as experimental design, quality control, read alignment, quantification, visualization, differential expression, alternative splicing, functional analysis, fusion detection and eQTL mapping [3].

6.1 Raw data and quality control

The sequencer’s output is FASTQ files: each read’s letters plus a per-base quality score. A Phred score of Q30 means a 1-in-1,000 chance that a base call is wrong.

Task

Tools

Convert raw signal to FASTQ

bcl2fastq, BCL Convert (Illumina)*

Read QC reports

FastQC*; MultiQC [14] aggregates reports across samples

Trimming and filtering

fastp [13]; also Trimmomatic*, Cutadapt*

Contamination screening

SortMeRNA*, Kraken2*, FastQ Screen*

Post-alignment QC

RSeQC*, Qualimap*, Picard*, samtools*

Tools marked with an asterisk are named from standard practice

MultiQC’s authors describe it as producing a single report that visualises output from many tools across many samples, so that global trends and biases are quickly spotted [14]. fastp performs quality control, adapter trimming and filtering in a single pass [13].

6.2 Getting from reads to genes: two strategies

Strategy A: align to the genome (splice-aware aligners). Reads from mature mRNA skip introns, so an aligner must split reads across exon–exon junctions.

  • STAR [6] was built to handle ENCODE-scale datasets. Its authors report that it aligns 550 million 2 × 76 bp paired-end reads per hour to the human genome on a modest 12-core server, over 50 times faster than other aligners at the time [6]. It is memory-hungry, typically needing tens of gigabytes of RAM for the human genome.

  • HISAT [7] and its successor HISAT2 [8] use hierarchical, graph-based FM indexes. HISAT was introduced as a fast spliced aligner with low memory requirements [7], and HISAT2 extends the approach to align against a graph that includes known genetic variants [8].

  • Alignments are stored as BAM files. featureCounts then assigns reads to genes. Its authors report it is an order of magnitude faster than earlier methods for gene-level summarisation and needs far less memory [11]. Annotation (GTF files) comes from Ensembl, GENCODE or RefSeq.

Strategy B: pseudoalignment / quasi-mapping. These tools skip full alignment and estimate how many reads came from each transcript.

  • Salmon combines a dual-phase inference algorithm, bias models and fast read mapping. It was the first transcriptome-wide quantifier to correct for fragment GC-content bias, which improves abundance estimates and downstream differential expression [9]. Its selective alignment mode was developed to overcome the shortcomings of lightweight mapping without the cost of full alignment [30].

  • kallisto pseudoaligns reads to a reference and lists the transcripts compatible with each read, avoiding base-by-base alignment. Its authors reported that 30 million paired-end reads can be analysed in under 10 minutes on a standard laptop [10].

  • Transcript-level estimates are summarised to genes with the R package tximport, which showed that transcript-level estimates improve gene-level inference [12].

Many pipelines combine both strategies, for example STAR alignments for QC and visualisation with Salmon for quantification. The community nf-core/rnaseq workflow supports this combination [15].

6.3 Reference genome and annotation

Using a mismatched or outdated genome and annotation is a common source of silent errors. For organisms with no reference genome, a transcriptome can be assembled de novo (for example with Trinity*), a possibility Wang and colleagues already emphasised for non-model organisms [1].

7. Normalisation and differential expression

Raw counts cannot be compared directly. A sample sequenced twice as deeply has about twice the counts, and longer genes yield more reads. Normalisation corrects for these effects.

  • RPKM/FPKM [2] and TPM adjust for gene length and library size. They are useful for descriptive comparisons but are not the input for statistical testing.

  • Between-sample methods such as the median-of-ratios method (DESeq2) [16] and TMM (edgeR) [18] correct for differences in library composition.

The statistical challenge is that counts are discrete, span a large dynamic range, include outliers, and often come from few replicates [16]. The dominant solutions model counts with a negative binomial distribution and borrow information across genes:

  • DESeq2 uses shrinkage estimation of dispersions and fold changes to improve stability and interpretability, and fits generalised linear models so complex designs can be handled [16].

  • edgeR uses an overdispersed Poisson/negative binomial model and moderates the overdispersion across transcripts with empirical Bayes methods, even with minimal replication [17].

  • limma-voom estimates the mean–variance relationship of log-counts, assigns a precision weight to each observation, and feeds these into limma’s empirical Bayes pipeline. The authors report accurate type I error control even with few samples, and the clear best performance of voom when sequencing depths differ between samples [19].

  • Schurch and colleagues concluded that edgeR and DESeq2 were the leading tools when fewer than twelve replicates were used [5].

Multiple testing. A genome-wide test examines about 20,000 genes at once, so p-values are adjusted for the false discovery rate (the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, reported as “padj” or “FDR”).

Batch effects. Variation from processing date, operator or lane can swamp biology. Remedies include including batch as a model covariate, or using sva*, ComBat-seq* or RUVSeq*. PCA and sample-distance heatmaps should always be inspected before testing.

8. From gene lists to biological questions

A list of 800 “differentially expressed genes” is not yet an answer. The next stage asks what those genes do.

8.1 Functional enrichment

  • Over-representation analysis asks whether a gene set (for example “cell cycle”) appears in the hit list more often than chance predicts. clusterProfiler 4.0 offers a universal interface for such analysis, covering thousands of organisms, with support for both over-representation and GSEA and for comparing results across gene lists [21]. Other web and R tools include g:Profiler*, DAVID* and Enrichr*, drawing on Gene Ontology*, KEGG*, Reactome* and MSigDB*.

  • Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) [20] works from the full ranked gene list rather than an arbitrary cutoff. It focuses on gene sets, groups of genes that share a biological function, chromosomal location or regulation. In the original paper it revealed pathways shared between two independent lung-cancer survival studies where single-gene analysis found little similarity [20].

  • A step-by-step protocol covers pathway enrichment analysis with g:Profiler, GSEA, Cytoscape and EnrichmentMap [22].

8.2 Co-expression and regulatory networks

WGCNA* groups genes with correlated expression into modules and relates those to traits. SCENIC* infers regulatory networks from single-cell data.

8.3 Splicing and isoforms

One gene can yield several transcripts. Long-read reviews note that short reads detect exon-level alternative splicing well but often cannot determine which full-length isoforms are expressed [29]. Short-read tools for splicing include rMATS*, DEXSeq*, LeafCutter*, MAJIQ*, SUPPA2* and DRIMSeq*. Differential transcript usage is a separate question from differential gene expression and needs separate testing.

8.4 Other questions RNA-seq can answer

  • Gene fusions in cancer (STAR-Fusion*, Arriba*).

  • Sequence variants and allele-specific expression from reads (GATK*). Wang and colleagues noted RNA-seq can reveal SNPs in transcribed regions [1].

  • eQTL mapping, linking genetic variants to expression (MatrixEQTL*, tensorQTL*). Conesa and colleagues discuss eQTL analysis as part of the workflow [3].

  • Cell-type deconvolution of bulk data (CIBERSORTx*, MuSiC*).

  • Small RNAs and circular RNAs (miRDeep2*, CIRCexplorer*).

  • Nascent RNA, translation and RNA structure, which Stark and colleagues list as adaptations of the core technology [4].

9. Single-cell RNA-seq analysis

In bulk RNA-seq a tumour’s signal is an average over thousands of cells. Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) shows which cells are present and what each is doing. Stark and colleagues describe the principle: cells are isolated, mRNA is reverse transcribed with cDNA typically tagged with UMIs, and libraries are sequenced [4].

The data form a count matrix (genes × cells). Luecken and Theis frame analysis as pre-processing (quality control, normalisation, data correction, feature selection and dimensionality reduction) followed by cell- and gene-level downstream analysis [23]. They also document the field’s sprawl, counting 385 analysis tools as of March 2019 [23].

Step

Typical tools

Reads → count matrix

Cell Ranger*, STARsolo*, alevin-fry*, kallisto-bustools*

Ambient RNA, doublets

CellBender*, SoupX*, Scrublet*

QC filters

Genes/UMIs per cell, mitochondrial fraction (dying cells)

Seurat [26], Scanpy [25], scran*

CellChat*, NicheNet*, LIANA*

Scanpy was built to scale to datasets of up to a million cells and provides preprocessing, visualisation, clustering, pseudotime and trajectory inference, and differential expression [25]. Seurat has evolved through several versions covering spatial reconstruction, integration across conditions and technologies, and multimodal analysis [26].

10. Long-read RNA-seq analysis

Because reads cover whole transcripts, the focus shifts to isoform discovery and quantification.

  • Basecalling: Dorado* (ONT). Circular consensus: SMRT Link/Iso-Seq tools* (PacBio).

  • Alignment: minimap2 [28], which does split-read alignment and was the first RNA-seq aligner designed specifically for long noisy reads [28].

  • Isoform discovery and quantification: StringTie2*, FLAIR*, Bambu*, IsoQuant*, TALON*.

  • Isoform QC: SQANTI3*.

  • Modification detection (direct RNA): m6Anet*, xPore*.

Challenges include higher per-base error rates (especially older nanopore chemistries), RNA degradation producing truncated reads, and a lack of settled statistics for differential isoform usage [29].

11. Spatial transcriptomics analysis

Spatial data add an (x, y) position to each expression profile. Typical tools are Space Ranger* (10x), Squidpy*, Seurat [26], cell2location*, RCTD* and Tangram* for deconvolving multi-cell spots, and BayesSpace* for spatial clustering. Imaging-based methods (MERFISH, Xenium, CosMx) need cell-segmentation tools such as Cellpose* or Baysor*.

12. Reproducibility and data sharing

  • Workflow managers: Nextflow with the community-curated nf-core framework, whose stated aim is standardised, portable, reproducible pipelines [15], plus Snakemake* and Galaxy*. Containers (Docker, Singularity/Apptainer) and Bioconda* freeze software versions.

  • Public repositories: raw data to NCBI SRA or ENA, processed matrices and metadata to GEO or ArrayExpress.

  • Report everything: genome and annotation versions, tool versions, parameters, filtering thresholds and sample metadata. Conesa and colleagues emphasise quality control at multiple stages for reproducibility and reliability [3].

13. A worked example, end to end

Suppose a lab wants to know how a drug changes gene expression in human lung-cancer cells (treated vs control, six replicates each).

  1. Design: 12 independent cultures, processing randomised across days; RIN ≥ 8; poly(A) selection with a stranded kit and ERCC spike-ins. Six replicates follow Schurch et al. [5].

  2. Sequence: pool onto a NovaSeq X 10B flow cell at 2 × 100 bp, aiming for about 30 million read pairs per sample [4, 31].

  3. QC: fastp [13] → FastQC* → MultiQC [14]; verify sample identity and rRNA content.

  4. Quantify: Salmon [9, 30] against GENCODE*; STAR [6] alignments in parallel for QC and genome-browser inspection. Or run nf-core/rnaseq [15].

  5. Import: tximport [12] into R.

  6. Explore: PCA and sample-distance heatmaps; look for batch effects.

  7. Test: DESeq2 [16] with ~ batch + treatment; apply fold-change shrinkage; threshold on FDR < 0.05 plus a sensible effect size.

  8. Interpret: GSEA [20] on the ranked list, clusterProfiler [21] for over-representation, rMATS* for splicing.

  9. Validate: confirm key genes by RT-qPCR or at the protein level.

  10. Deposit: FASTQ to SRA, counts to GEO, code and environment files to a public repository.

14. Limitations and honest caveats

  • RNA-seq measures RNA, not protein. Transcript levels only partly predict protein levels.

  • Bulk data average over cell populations, so changes in cell composition can masquerade as changes in expression.

  • Short reads cannot resolve many isoforms [29], and GC and fragmentation biases exist [9].

  • Platform differences are small but real. One core facility advises against switching sequencers mid-project [34].

  • Statistical significance is not biological importance. With enough samples, tiny changes become significant.

  • Tools evolve quickly. A review counted hundreds of single-cell tools within a few years [23], so best practice keeps moving. Check current benchmarks before fixing a pipeline.

15. Looking ahead

Active frontiers include long-read single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, direct RNA sequencing for RNA modifications, and ever-cheaper short-read platforms from multiple vendors. A recent review summarises long-read transcriptomics as moving toward single-cell, spatial, direct RNA and multi-omics applications [38].

title: Why antimicrobial resistance is a One Health problem
summary: Antimicrobial resistance connects human health, animal health, food systems, and the environment.
body:
In brief

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) happens when bacteria, fungi, viruses and parasites evolve so that the medicines meant to kill them stop working. It is often discussed as a hospital problem. The scientific literature shows it is bigger than that. The same resistant bacteria, the same resistance genes, and the same drivers (antimicrobial use and pollution) move between people, farm animals, crops, soil, rivers and wastewater. Because resistance does not respect the boundaries between these systems, no single sector, whether medicine, veterinary science, agriculture or environmental protection, can solve it alone. That is the core argument for treating AMR as a One Health problem.

This essay explains the concept, lays out the evidence for each link between humans, animals and the environment, and also describes where the evidence is uncertain, because honest uncertainty is part of the science.

1. What "One Health" means

In 2021 an expert panel convened by four UN-system organisations (FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH, together called the Quadripartite) published a formal definition. One Health is an integrated, unifying approach that aims to balance and optimise the health of people, animals and ecosystems, recognising that the health of humans, domestic and wild animals, plants and the wider environment is closely linked and interdependent [1]. In practice it means that sectors that rarely talk to each other (doctors, vets, farmers, water engineers, ecologists, regulators) have to plan together.

AMR is one of the topics the One Health framework was built to address, alongside zoonotic diseases (infections passing from animals to people) and food safety.

2. Why AMR matters: the scale of the problem

The best global estimates come from the Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance (GRAM) project. Its first analysis, published in The Lancet in 2022, estimated that bacterial AMR was directly responsible for about 1.27 million deaths in 2019 and was associated with about 4.95 million deaths, meaning resistant infection played some role [2]. A follow-up covering 1990 to 2021 and forecasting to 2050 estimated 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR in 2021 and 4.71 million associated deaths [3]. The 2021 figures were lower than 2019, which the authors linked to reduced burden from some respiratory infections during COVID-19 distancing rather than to any real improvement in resistance [3].

Some key findings of that study [3]:

  • Deaths from AMR in children under five fell by more than half between 1990 and 2021, probably thanks to better infection prevention and care.

  • Deaths in people aged 70 and over rose by more than 80% over the same period.

  • Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) deaths more than doubled, from about 57,000 to about 130,000.

  • Deaths from carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections rose from about 127,000 to about 216,000. Carbapenems are "last-resort" antibiotics.

  • On current trends, the authors forecast about 1.91 million attributable and 8.22 million associated deaths per year by 2050, and more than 39 million cumulative attributable deaths between 2025 and 2050.

These are model-based estimates built from patchy data, particularly in low-income countries, so the uncertainty ranges are wide. But the direction is consistent across studies.

3. The basic biology: why resistance is shared

Bacteria become resistant in two main ways. First, mutations in their own DNA can change the target of a drug or how much of it gets in. Second, and more relevant to One Health, bacteria can acquire resistance genes from other bacteria by horizontal gene transfer. These genes often sit on mobile DNA elements such as plasmids, small circular DNA molecules that can be copied from one cell to another, even across species. A useful analogy: mutation is like a person inventing a trick on their own, while horizontal gene transfer is like handing the trick around the neighbourhood.

This is why the habitat of a bacterium matters less than one might think. A resistance gene that arises in a soil microbe, a pig's gut or a patient's gut can, in principle, end up in a pathogen elsewhere. A landmark study by Forsberg and colleagues cultured bacteria from soil and found resistance genes against five antibiotic classes (β-lactams, aminoglycosides, amphenicols, sulfonamides and tetracyclines) that were identical at the DNA level to genes in human pathogens, including the surrounding non-coding sequences and mobilisation elements. That is strong evidence of recent gene exchange between environmental bacteria and clinical pathogens [16]. The study could not tell in which direction the genes had moved, which is a recurring limitation in this field.

Resistance is also ancient. Most antibiotics used in medicine originate from soil microbes, which use them to compete with each other, so environmental bacteria have long had the genes to defend themselves. Larsson and Flach, in a comprehensive review in Nature Reviews Microbiology, describe the environment as a vast reservoir of resistance genes. New resistance factors reach pathogens only through rare evolutionary events that are difficult to predict but can have enormous consequences once they occur. They also argue that the environment may already harbour resistance genes against essentially any antibiotic we could develop [17].

4. The genetic machinery: resistance genes and mobile elements

Resistance travels at three nested levels: the resistance gene, the mobile DNA element that carries it, and the bacterium that hosts it. The One Health evidence appears at every level.

Resistance genes and what they do

An antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) is a stretch of DNA that lets a microbe survive a drug. Genes work in different ways. Some encode enzymes that destroy the drug, such as the CTX-M β-lactamases, which break down expanded-spectrum cephalosporins [29]. Others alter the drug's target. MCR-1 is an enzyme that adds a phosphoethanolamine group to lipid A, a component of the outer membrane that colistin acts on [8]. In fungi, the dominant azole-resistance genotype of Aspergillus fumigatus, TR34/L98H, combines a 34-base-pair repeat in the promoter of the cyp51A gene, which raises its expression, with an amino-acid substitution in the protein [23]. The full collection of ARGs in a community of microbes is called its resistome.

Mobile genetic elements: the delivery vehicles

Bacteria carry resistance genes on pieces of DNA that can move. The main types discussed in the literature are:

  • Plasmids: small circular DNA molecules that copy themselves and can be passed from one bacterium to another, sometimes across species.

  • Insertion sequences and transposons: short DNA segments, often called "jumping genes", that can cut or copy themselves into new locations and can carry neighbouring genes with them.

  • Integrons: genetic platforms that capture and line up "gene cassettes" so that they are expressed from a shared promoter [30].

Other vehicles, such as integrative conjugative elements and bacteriophages (viruses of bacteria), also move genes between cells.

What the studies show

  • Gene capture from the environment. CTX-M enzymes, the most widespread family of extended-spectrum β-lactamases, did not evolve step by step from earlier plasmid enzymes. Phylogenetic analyses indicate that they derive from chromosomal genes of environmental Kluyvera bacteria, which were captured by insertion sequences such as ISEcp1 and ISCR1 and moved onto plasmids. In silico analyses suggest this capture happened at least nine separate times [29].

  • Plasmid transfer of a last-resort resistance gene. The mcr-1 plasmid from the first pig isolate moved into an E. coli recipient at a frequency of 10⁻¹ to 10⁻³ per recipient cell and was maintained in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa [8]. In a later survey of mcr-1-positive E. coli, 92% of the gene copies were on plasmids, and three plasmid types (IncX4, IncI2 and IncHI2) accounted for 76% [10]. After China's colistin ban, the study recorded shifts in the plasmid types and in the DNA flanking mcr-1, showing that the mobile elements themselves keep evolving after a policy change [10].

  • Integrons as pollution markers. The class 1 integron found in clinical bacteria is thought to have arisen when a chromosomal integron from an environmental bacterium was captured by a transposon, picking up cassettes for disinfectant (qacE) and sulphonamide (sul1) resistance. This hybrid element has since captured at least 130 different resistance cassettes. Because its integrase gene, intI1, is linked to genes for resistance to antibiotics, disinfectants and heavy metals, and rises with human impact, Gillings and colleagues proposed it as a proxy for anthropogenic pollution [30].

  • Gene exchange between soil and clinic. The soil genes found identical to those in human pathogens came with identical flanking and mobilisation sequences, evidence of a route by which they spread [16].

  • Mobile elements in polluted rivers. River sediment downstream of the Indian drug-manufacturing plant held many resistance genes together with gene transfer elements [19]. Larsson and Flach conclude that selection pressure from antibiotics has promoted the mobilisation and horizontal transfer of a wide range of ARGs [17].
