Why this matters for One Health

  1. Genes can spread without strains, and strains without genes spreading further. A resistance gene can hop between bacterial species, so tracking only bacterial isolates can miss sharing, while finding the same gene in two places does not prove the same strain moved between them. This is why the Dutch studies compared both gene types and plasmid replicon types across human, animal, food and environmental reservoirs [14][15].

  2. Non-antibiotic pollutants may matter. Because class 1 integrons are linked to resistance to disinfectants and heavy metals as well as antibiotics, the review by Gillings and colleagues argues that this wider pollution is relevant to the persistence of these elements [30].

  3. Gene-based surveillance is possible but needs care. Measuring ARGs and markers such as intI1 in sewage or rivers can complement clinical surveillance [17][24][30]. Detecting a gene in a metagenome does not by itself show that it sits in a pathogen, is expressed, or poses a clinical risk, and Larsson and Flach give a critical account of the methods and their limits [17].

5. The human link: how we use antibiotics

Human medicine is a major driver. Using sales data from 76 countries, Klein and colleagues found that global antibiotic consumption rose 65% between 2000 and 2015, from 21.1 to 34.8 billion defined daily doses [4]. Most of the growth came from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where consumption rose 114% overall, linked to economic growth and improved access. In high-income countries total consumption rose only about 6% and the per-capita rate fell about 4%. The study also reported rapid growth in use of last-resort drugs such as carbapenems and polymyxins, and projected that, without policy change, consumption could be up to 200% higher by 2030 [4].

Two points deserve emphasis. First, many LMICs still use fewer antibiotics per person than rich countries despite a higher burden of bacterial infection, so reducing use must be balanced against access, since millions of people die from lack of effective treatment. Second, because patients, hospitals and communities are connected to sewage systems, farms and rivers, what happens inside the clinic does not stay in the clinic.

6. The animal link: livestock, aquaculture and companion animals

How much is used

Antimicrobials have been used in animal farming for decades, for treating sick animals, preventing disease in groups, and in some countries for growth promotion. A modelling study by Mulchandani and colleagues estimated global antimicrobial use in food-producing animals at about 99,500 tonnes in 2020, projected to reach about 107,500 tonnes by 2030 (an 8% rise), with usage hotspots concentrated in Asia (about 67%) and under 1% in Africa [6]. An earlier analysis in Science concluded that antimicrobial consumption in animals is roughly three times that in humans, and a widely quoted estimate attributes about 73% of global antibiotic use to animals raised for meat [5][7]. These are modelled estimates, because many countries do not report veterinary use, but they indicate the scale.

Resistance is rising in animals

Van Boeckel and colleagues compiled 901 point-prevalence surveys from LMICs and mapped resistance in four pathogens (E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella and S. aureus). Between 2000 and 2018, the proportion of antimicrobial compounds with resistance above 50% rose from about 0.15 to 0.41 in chickens and from about 0.13 to 0.34 in pigs [7]. The authors warned that escalating resistance in animals would be expected to matter for animal health and, eventually, for human health, and proposed that a transition to more sustainable farming, supported by wealthier countries, could limit the rise [7].

A case study: mcr-1 and colistin

The clearest single example linking farms and hospitals is mcr-1. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic for infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Until 2015, colistin resistance was known only through chromosomal mutations, which do not spread easily. Then Liu and colleagues, doing routine surveillance of farm animals in China, found a plasmid-borne gene, mcr-1, that could transfer between bacteria and made E. coli resistant to colistin. In their sampling from 2011 to 2014, the gene was found in about 15% of raw meat samples, 21% of animals, and 1% of hospital inpatient samples [8]. The authors suggested that the gene likely originated in animals and spread to people, and that the rate in hospital patients was lower than in animals, consistent with that direction of travel. China was a major user of colistin in agriculture at the time. Since then, mcr genes have been reported in humans, animals and meat in more than 50 countries on six continents [9].

China banned colistin as a growth promoter in animal feed on 30 April 2017 (therapeutic use was not banned). Studies afterwards documented large effects:

  • Production of colistin sulfate premix for feed fell from 27,170 tonnes in 2015 to 2,497 tonnes in 2018, and the researchers reported reductions in colistin resistance in animals and humans [9].

  • In national pig farm sampling, mcr-1 prevalence fell from 45% of samples in 2016 to 19% in 2018 [10].

  • In hospital inpatients, mcr-1 colonisation fell to near pre-2015 levels after the ban, although it remained somewhat higher than in 2011 to 2013, possibly because colistin was approved for human clinical use in China in January 2017 [11].

This is not a perfect experiment. Other changes were happening at the same time, hospital-origin strains seemed less affected by the ban than community strains [10], and the authors themselves noted that the ban might not be the only explanation [9]. Even so, it is among the best real-world evidence that a policy in the animal sector can reduce resistance in people, which is the One Health premise in action.

What systematic reviews say

A systematic review and meta-analysis commissioned by the WHO examined 181 studies on restricting antibiotic use in food animals. Interventions that restricted use were associated with a reduction in resistant bacteria in animals, typically by about 10 to 15 percentage points. In human studies, pooled resistance prevalence was about 24% lower in groups exposed to such interventions, with a stronger association among people in direct contact with food animals. The authors cautioned that implications for the general population were less clear because only a small number of studies were available [12]. These findings underpinned the WHO's 2017 guidelines, which recommend an overall reduction in medically important antimicrobial use in food-producing animals, and complete restriction of use for growth promotion and for disease prevention in animals that have not been diagnosed as sick [13]. As a real-world illustration, Denmark ended growth-promoter use in 1999 and, according to figures reported alongside the guidelines, saw animal antibiotic consumption fall by 49% since 1994 while meat production rose by 15% [27].

7. Nuance: how much resistance flows from animals to people?

A fair One Health essay has to say that the size of animal-to-human transmission is debated, and that it differs by pathogen and setting.

A modelling study in the Netherlands attributed the sources of community carriage of ESBL- and pAmpC-producing E. coli (bacteria resistant to important β-lactam antibiotics). It found that human-to-human transmission within the community accounted for about 60% of carriage, with the rest coming from other sources including food, farm animals, companion animals, wild birds, and surface water. The authors calculated that intracommunity spread alone would not be self-sustaining (a reproduction number below 1, about 0.63), so exchange with non-human sources appears to be needed to maintain it [14]. A separate pooled analysis of 35 Dutch studies found very close similarity of ESBL/AmpC genes between farmers and their animals, but much lower similarity between livestock or food and people in the general population, and it did not demonstrate a close link between livestock farms and the general population [15].

These results do not undermine One Health. They show that the connections are real but unevenly strong, that some people (farmers, veterinarians, abattoir workers, travellers) are more exposed than others, and that humans are themselves a major reservoir. That is exactly why integrated surveillance of people, animals, food and environments is needed to measure the flows rather than assume them.

8. The environmental link: where the pathways meet

The environment is not just a passive backdrop. Larsson and Flach identify three roles: it is a reservoir of resistance genes, a site where resistance can evolve (when antibiotic pollution selects for resistant bacteria and for mobile genetic elements), and a transmission route between hosts. In many places it also simply reflects the regional clinical resistance situation, which makes it useful for surveillance [17].

Wastewater and faecal pollution

Human and animal waste carries both resistant bacteria and antibiotic residues into sewage, rivers and soil. One analysis of antibiotic resistance genes in human-impacted environments concluded that faecal pollution explained much of the variation in resistance gene abundance [21]. Experimental work has shown that even sterile-filtered hospital wastewater can select for multidrug-resistant E. coli, probably because of the mixture of antibiotics and other compounds it contains [20]. Because of this, there are active proposals to monitor resistance in sewage. Larsson, Flach and Laxminarayan discuss a proposed European Union requirement to monitor resistance at sewage treatment plants serving more than 100,000 people, and note both the opportunities and the challenges [24].

Pollution from drug manufacturing

The most extreme environmental cases come from antibiotic production. In 2007 Larsson and colleagues analysed effluent from a treatment plant serving about 90 bulk-drug manufacturers near Hyderabad, India. It contained the highest pharmaceutical concentrations ever reported in an effluent, with the antibiotic ciprofloxacin reaching up to 31,000 micrograms per litre, which is more than 1,000 times the level toxic to some bacteria [18]. Later sequencing of river sediment downstream found very high levels of ciprofloxacin and a high prevalence of resistance genes against multiple antibiotic classes, along with gene transfer elements [19]. The study showed that industrial pollution can create conditions in which resistance is strongly selected. In its 2024 political commitments and guidance, the international community has recognised manufacturing pollution as an issue to address [25].

Agriculture beyond livestock: the fungal example

AMR is not limited to antibiotics and bacteria. Azole chemicals are used as antifungal drugs in people, as fungicides on crops, and in materials such as timber preservatives. Fisher and colleagues reviewed how this multiple use has driven independent evolution of resistance in many environments and described an unprecedented rate of emergence of resistant fungal pathogens [22]. The mould Aspergillus fumigatus, which can cause life-threatening lung disease in immunocompromised patients, carries two dominant azole-resistance mechanisms (TR34/L98H and TR46/Y121F/T289A) thought to have arisen under agricultural azole selection. A global genetic analysis of 4,049 isolates found identical resistant clones in both clinical and environmental samples worldwide [23]. A patient can thus acquire a resistant fungus from the environment without ever having taken the drug, which is a vivid example of why human medicine alone cannot control resistance.

9. How resistance spreads between people, animals and the environment

Resistance spreads whenever resistant bacteria, or the genes they carry, are carried from one host or habitat to another. Three things can move: the bacteria themselves (clonal spread), the mobile elements and genes they hold (see section 4), and the antibiotic pollution that selects for resistance. The literature describes the following routes, which are not all equally well quantified.

  1. Direct contact between animals and people. In the Dutch pooled analysis, ESBL/AmpC genes in farmers closely matched those in their broilers and pigs [15]. The WHO-commissioned meta-analysis likewise found a stronger association between restricting animal antibiotic use and lower resistance in people with direct contact with food animals [12]. Farmers are treated as a high-risk group in source-attribution models [14].

  2. The food chain. Resistant bacteria and genes reach people via meat and other foods. Liu and colleagues found mcr-1 in about 15% of raw meat samples tested in China [8], and food is one of the sources in the Dutch model [14]. The evidence is mixed, however: the pooled Dutch analysis found much lower gene similarity between livestock or food and people in the general population than between farmers and their animals [15].

  3. Wastewater, surface water and drinking water. Human and animal faeces carry resistant bacteria and antibiotic residues into sewage, rivers and soil [17][21]. Hospital wastewater can select for multidrug-resistant E. coli [20]. Near the Indian manufacturing hub, pollution reached surface, ground and drinking water [19].

  4. Soil and crops. Soil bacteria and pathogens share identical resistance genes with mobilisation sequences [16]. For fungi, azole fungicides on crops select resistant Aspergillus fumigatus, so patients can be infected with a resistant fungus from the environment [22][23].

  5. Person-to-person spread, including in hospitals and communities. The Dutch model attributed about 60% of community ESBL/AmpC E. coli carriage to human-to-human transmission [14]. Hospital patients can acquire resistant strains: mcr-1 was found in about 1% of inpatient samples in the first Chinese study [8].

  6. Wildlife and companion animals. The Dutch source-attribution data included companion animals, wild birds and surface freshwater among the sources of resistance genes found in people [14].

  7. Travel and trade. Returning travellers were a high-risk group in the Dutch data, and the authors list human mobility and trade in goods among the factors involved [14]. The discoverers of mcr-1 expected it to follow other resistance genes such as blaNDM-1 around the world [8], and mcr genes have since been found in more than 50 countries on six continents [9]. Fisher and colleagues describe resistant fungi spreading along human globalisation routes in a similar way [22].

Two cautions apply. First, the direction of transfer is usually inferred rather than observed. The authors of the mcr-1 paper reasoned from the lower share in patients than in animals that the gene probably started in animals [8], and the soil-pathogen study could not say which way its genes had moved [16]. Second, human-to-human spread appears dominant for some resistant E. coli, yet the Dutch modelling suggests that spread within the community alone would not sustain itself without input from non-human sources [14]. That combination, rather than any single route, is the case for managing all sectors together.

10. Putting the pieces together: why "One Health" is the right frame

The literature supports five reasons to treat AMR as a One Health problem.

  1. Shared drivers. Antimicrobial use in medicine, veterinary practice, aquaculture and crop protection all exert selection pressure, and pollution from hospitals, farms and factories spreads that pressure into the environment [4][6][17].

  2. Shared genes and bacteria. Mobile resistance genes and some resistant strains circulate across human, animal and environmental compartments, as shown by identical genes in soil bacteria and pathogens [16] and by mcr-1 in pigs, meat and patients [8].

  3. Shared pathways. Food, water, soil, wastewater, wildlife, trade and travel connect the compartments, and the Dutch ESBL work suggests that persistence of resistance in a community may depend on both human-to-human and non-human sources [14].

  4. Interventions in one sector affect others. The colistin ban in Chinese agriculture was followed by falls in resistance in animals and in people [9][10][11], and meta-analytic evidence links restrictions on animal use with lower resistance in animals and, more modestly, in exposed humans [12].

  5. Unequal exposure and responsibility. Antibiotic consumption is converging between rich and poor countries [4], animal-use hotspots are concentrated in Asia [6], and the burden of deaths is heavy where access to clean water, diagnostics and effective treatment is weakest [3]. The problem is global, so a purely national or single-sector response leaves gaps.

It follows that effective responses must combine measures such as infection prevention and control, clean water and sanitation, vaccination, better diagnostics, prudent antibiotic use in all sectors, controls on manufacturing and waste, integrated surveillance, and development of new drugs and alternatives, while preserving fair access to the medicines people need.

11. Policy: where the world stands

Governments have increasingly adopted the One Health framing. At the UN General Assembly high-level meeting in September 2024, world leaders approved a political declaration with a target of reducing global deaths associated with bacterial AMR by 10% by 2030 (relative to the 4.95 million estimate for 2019), a goal that at least 70% of antibiotics used in human health come from the WHO "Access" group, a call for US$100 million in catalytic funding, a target that at least 60% of countries have funded national AMR action plans, commitments to reduce antimicrobial use in agri-food systems, and recognition of antimicrobial pollution in the environment. It also asked for an Independent Panel on Evidence for Action against AMR, a body that is often compared to the IPCC for climate change, and for the Global Action Plan to be updated by 2026 [25]. On 23 May 2026 the World Health Assembly adopted the updated Global Action Plan on AMR 2026 to 2036, framed as a One Health plan that builds on the 2024 commitments [26]. Press reports from November 2026 say the Independent Panel is expected to be launched at a global meeting in Abuja, Nigeria, around World AMR Awareness Week (18 to 24 November) [28]. Readers should check the latest status, as such plans move quickly.

Critics note that the 10% target is modest and that progress will be hard to measure, particularly where surveillance is weak. Targets alone also do not guarantee funding or implementation.

12. What remains uncertain

A technical reader should know where the field's open questions lie:

  • Quantifying transmission. Source-attribution studies exist for a few bacteria and countries but not for most settings, and results vary by organism, gene and population [14][15].

  • Direction of gene flow. Identical genes in the environment and in clinical bacteria show exchange but usually not the direction or timing [16].

  • Data gaps. Veterinary and environmental data, and clinical data from LMICs, are sparse, so global burden and animal-use figures are modelled estimates with wide uncertainty [3][6].

  • Selection thresholds. What concentrations of antibiotics in the environment select for resistance is still being worked out, and standardised methods are being developed [17].

  • Policy impact. Natural experiments such as the colistin ban are encouraging but can be confounded by other changes [9][10][11].

13. Why it matters to you

Resistant infections make routine medical care riskier, including surgery, cancer chemotherapy, caesarean sections and joint replacement, because these depend on antibiotics that work. Individuals can help by using antibiotics only when prescribed, finishing courses as directed by their clinician, not demanding them for viral illnesses, keeping vaccinations up to date, washing hands and handling food safely, and supporting policies on farming, sanitation and pollution. The scientific consensus is that these actions are needed across all sectors at once. That is the meaning of One Health.

Glossary

  • Antimicrobial: a medicine that kills or inhibits microbes. Antibiotics are the antibacterial subset.

  • Attributable deaths: deaths that would not have happened if the infection had been treatable. Associated deaths are those where a resistant infection was present, even if resistance was not the only cause.

  • Plasmid: a small, mobile loop of DNA that can carry resistance genes between bacteria.

  • Horizontal gene transfer: the passing of genes between bacteria that are not parent and offspring.

  • Resistome: the full collection of resistance genes in a community of microbes.

  • Zoonosis: an infection that passes between animals and humans.

title: How do vaccines create immune memory?
summary: Vaccines prepare the immune system to respond more effectively to a future encounter with a pathogen or antigen. - Coming Soon
body: Vaccines expose the immune system to an antigen or instructions for making one, in a form intended to generate protective immunity without causing the target disease. Antigen-presenting cells help activate lymphocytes, and some activated B and T cells develop into long-lived memory populations. The strength and duration of protection depend on the vaccine platform, antigen, host, and pathogen.

title: CRISPR: a programmable tool for biological research
summary: CRISPR-based systems let researchers target particular DNA sequences to study gene function and more.
body:
Think of the genome as a very long book with three billion letters. For most of the twentieth century, biologists could read it, and they could sometimes smash a page or two, but editing a specific sentence on purpose was slow, expensive and unreliable. CRISPR changed that. It works a bit like a find-and-replace function: you give it a short address written in RNA, and a protein goes to the matching place in the DNA and does something there. The something can be cutting, switching a gene off, switching it on, or rewriting a single letter. The address is cheap to make, which is why a technique that appeared in its modern form in 2012 is now routine in thousands of labs.

This essay covers where CRISPR came from, how it works, what you need to run an experiment, what researchers have done with it, where it has reached patients, and where it still falls short. I have tried to stick to what is published and to cite it. Clinical news moves quickly, so check the primary sources before relying on any single number.

Where it came from

CRISPR was not invented. It was found, slowly, and for years nobody knew what it was for.

In 1987 a Japanese group led by Yoshizumi Ishino was sequencing a gene in E. coli and noticed something odd next to it: five short, nearly identical stretches of DNA separated by unrelated spacer sequences [1]. They had no explanation and the observation sat largely uncited for years. Over the 1990s and early 2000s, Francisco Mojica at the University of Alicante found similar repeats in archaea and many bacteria, and in 2002, in correspondence with Ruud Jansen, helped settle on the name CRISPR, short for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. Jansen also noticed a set of conserved genes sitting beside the repeats, the cas (CRISPR-associated) genes [3].

The turning point came in 2005, when Mojica and others showed that many of the spacers matched DNA from bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) and plasmids [2]. That suggested the repeat array was a kind of memory of past invaders. Roughly 40% of sequenced bacterial genomes, and about 90% of archaeal ones, carry at least one CRISPR locus [3].

The proof arrived in 2007. Rodolphe Barrangou and colleagues, working at the yogurt company Danisco, infected Streptococcus thermophilus with phage and showed that survivors had picked up new spacers from the phage genome, and that these spacers decided which phages the bacteria could resist [4]. In 2008 Brouns and colleagues showed that the CRISPR transcripts are cut into small guide RNAs [5], and Marraffini and Sontheimer showed that the target is DNA, not RNA, using a Staphylococcus epidermidis system that blocked plasmid transfer [6]. In 2011 Deltcheva and colleagues, in Emmanuelle Charpentier's lab, found that the type II system needs a second small RNA, the tracrRNA, to process its guides [7].

The pivotal paper came in 2012. Martin Jinek, Krzysztof Chylinski, Ines Fonfara, Michael Hauer, Jennifer Doudna and Charpentier showed that purified Cas9 protein, paired with a crRNA and tracrRNA, cuts DNA at a site set by the RNA sequence, with one nuclease domain (HNH) cutting one strand and the other (RuvC-like) cutting the opposite strand [9]. They also fused the two RNAs into a single guide RNA (sgRNA) and showed it worked just as well, and they pointed out the potential for RNA-programmable genome editing. A Lithuanian group led by Virginijus Šikšnys reported closely related biochemistry in the same period [8].

Six months later, in January 2013, two papers showed the system worked in human cells. Cong and colleagues in Feng Zhang's lab edited human and mouse cells and showed that several guides could be used at once [10]. Mali and colleagues in George Church's lab did it with a two-component version and computed roughly 190,000 guide sequences covering about 40% of human exons [11]. After that, adoption was fast. Doudna and Charpentier received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the method [51].

How it works

The most widely used system, SpCas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes, has two parts you need to know about.

The protein (Cas9) is the cutter. It has two nuclease domains, HNH and RuvC, and each cuts one strand of the DNA double helix [9].

The guide RNA (sgRNA) is the address. Its first 20 or so nucleotides are the part you design. They are complementary to the DNA you want to hit. The rest of the RNA folds into a scaffold that Cas9 holds on to [9, 12].

The search works in two steps. Cas9 does not read the whole genome looking for a 20-letter match. It first scans for a short motif called the PAM (protospacer adjacent motif), which for SpCas9 is NGG, meaning any base followed by two Gs. Only next to a PAM does Cas9 start prying the DNA open and testing whether the guide base-pairs with it. If the match is good, the DNA forms a structure called an R-loop and both strands are cut, producing a blunt break about three base pairs from the PAM [13]. The PAM requirement is why you cannot target literally any position: the site has to sit next to the right motif. Structures of Cas9 show how the RNA reshapes the protein into its active form [14].

Once the DNA is cut, the cell has to fix it, and the way it fixes it determines the experimental outcome [13, 15]:

  • Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) glues the ends back together quickly but sloppily, often adding or deleting a few letters (indels). If this happens inside a gene, it frequently breaks the gene. This is the basis of most knockouts.

  • Homology-directed repair (HDR) copies from a template. If you supply a DNA template with your desired change, the cell may use it, letting you correct a mutation or insert a sequence. HDR is less efficient than NHEJ and works mainly in dividing cells.

That is the entire core idea: a programmable cut, plus the cell's own repair machinery doing the editing. Almost everything else in the field is a variation on it.

Beyond the basic cut

The cut-and-repair approach has a drawback, which is that double-strand breaks are messy. So researchers have built tools that use the same addressing system for other jobs.

Other Cas enzymes. Cas12a (formerly Cpf1) uses a single RNA, recognizes a different PAM, and leaves staggered ends [22]. Cas13 (formerly C2c2) targets RNA instead of DNA [23]. Both, once activated, also chew up nearby single-stranded nucleic acids indiscriminately, which turned out to be useful for diagnostics (below).

CRISPRi and CRISPRa. If you mutate both nuclease domains you get "dead" Cas9 (dCas9), which still binds DNA but does not cut. Qi and colleagues used it to block transcription [16]. Fused to a repressor or activator domain, it can turn genes down (CRISPRi) or up (CRISPRa) without changing the DNA sequence. Gilbert and colleagues reported typically 90 to 99% knockdown with CRISPRi and built genome-scale libraries for both [17].

Base editing. In 2016 Komor and colleagues fused a nickase or dead Cas9 to a deaminase enzyme to convert one base into another without a double-strand break [20]. Adenine and cytosine base editors now cover the common point mutations, which matter because many inherited diseases come from a single-letter change.

Prime editing. In 2019 Anzalone and colleagues described prime editing, in which a Cas9 nickase is fused to a reverse transcriptase and the desired edit is written into an extended guide called a pegRNA. It can make insertions, deletions and all 12 types of base substitution without double-strand breaks or donor DNA [21]. In human cells the authors reported editing efficiencies of 20 to 50% with 1 to 10% indels at the sites they tested, and estimated that in principle it could correct up to 89% of known disease-associated variants. It is better suited to small edits than to large insertions.

What you need to run an experiment

A CRISPR experiment has a design stage on a computer, a delivery stage at the bench, and a checking stage that is arguably the most important of the three.

Reagents

  • A nuclease or editor. SpCas9 is the default. You can deliver it as a plasmid, as mRNA, or as a pre-assembled protein-plus-guide complex called an RNP. High-fidelity variants, Cas12a, base editors and prime editors are chosen when the situation calls for them.

  • A guide RNA. Either encoded on a plasmid or lentiviral vector, or ordered as a synthetic RNA. For repair by HDR you also need a donor template.

  • A delivery method. Lipid-based transfection or electroporation for cultured cells, lentivirus for pooled screens and hard-to-transfect cells, microinjection for embryos, and, in animals and patients, viral vectors such as AAV or lipid nanoparticles (see the therapy section). Reviews of delivery compare these on efficiency, payload size and immune response [Lopes and Prasad, 43].

  • Controls and validation reagents. A non-targeting guide, a positive-control guide, and primers around the target for sequencing.

Software

Guide design is where most of the software comes in. A good design tool picks a guide with high predicted on-target activity and few similar sequences elsewhere in the genome.

Task

Tools

Notes

Guide design and scoring

CRISPOR [28], CHOPCHOP [29], Benchling

CRISPOR collects published on- and off-target scoring algorithms and supports a large number of genomes. CHOPCHOP is a web tool that also handles TALENs. Benchling is a commercial platform that also handles sequence design.

Off-target prediction

Cas-OFFinder [30]

Searches a genome for sites that resemble the guide, allowing mismatches.

On-target activity prediction

Rule Set 2 scores [31]

Built from large datasets of guide activity. Built into several design tools.

Experimental off-target detection

GUIDE-seq [32], Digenome-seq

Genome-wide, unbiased methods that identify real cutting in cells or in vitro, instead of predicting it.

Analysis of edited samples

CRISPResso2 [33]

Quantifies indels and precise edits from sequencing data. Sanger-trace tools such as TIDE and ICE are common for quick checks.

Pooled screen analysis

MAGeCK [34]

Statistical analysis of guide depletion or enrichment.

Hanna and Doench give a thorough overview of how to choose among these tools and what to look out for [35].

A practical point that beginners miss: predictions are only predictions. The design tools estimate where Cas9 might cut. Whether it actually does depends on the cell type, chromatin state and delivery method, so for anything that matters, you check with sequencing, and for therapeutic work you add unbiased off-target assays.

CRISPR as a research tool

For most scientists, CRISPR is a way of asking what a gene does by changing it.

Knockouts and model organisms. Before CRISPR, making a knockout mouse took months of work in embryonic stem cells. Injecting Cas9 and a guide into an embryo now produces edited animals directly, and the same approach works in zebrafish, flies, plants and many other organisms [13].

Genome-wide screens. Because guides are cheap to synthesize in bulk, you can build a library with several guides for every gene, put one guide into each cell of a population, apply a selection such as a drug or virus, and see by sequencing which guides are enriched or lost. In 2014 two papers did this in human cells. Shalem and colleagues used a library of 64,751 guides targeting 18,080 genes to identify genes essential for cell viability and genes involved in resistance to a melanoma drug [18]. Wang and colleagues used 73,000 guides to find essential genes and to identify genes needed for sensitivity to a nucleotide analog [19]. CRISPRi and CRISPRa screens followed [17].

Multiplexing. Several guides can be delivered together to edit multiple genes at once, which Cong and colleagues demonstrated in the first human-cell paper [10].

Imaging and recording. Dead Cas9 fused to a fluorescent protein has been used to visualize genomic loci in living cells, and CRISPR editing has been used as a molecular recorder of cell events [13].

Diagnostics. Cas12 and Cas13 do something unusual once they find their target: they begin cutting any nearby single-stranded DNA or RNA. Researchers put a fluorescent reporter into the mix and read the glow. Combined with an amplification step, the SHERLOCK method (Cas13) detected RNA at very low concentrations, and was used to distinguish Zika and dengue strains [24, 26]. DETECTR (Cas12a) did the same for DNA and was shown to differentiate types of human papillomavirus [25]. A third paper described a field-deployable version [27].

Agriculture. CRISPR has been used to edit crops for traits such as disease resistance and stress tolerance, and the regulatory treatment of edited plants differs between countries [47, 48].

Gene drives. A gene drive biases inheritance so that a trait spreads through a population faster than normal. In 2016 Hammond and colleagues built a CRISPR-based drive targeting female fertility genes in the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae [45]. Reviews describe the idea as promising for vector control but also point to unresolved technical, ethical and regulatory issues [46]. This remains a laboratory and policy question, not a deployed tool.

CRISPR as a medicine

There are two broad ways to treat a patient. In ex vivo therapy, cells are removed, edited in a dish, checked, and given back. In in vivo therapy, the editor is delivered into the body.

Ex vivo: Casgevy

Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia both come from mutations in the beta-globin gene. Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel, or exa-cel) does not repair that gene. Instead, the patient's blood stem cells are edited with Cas9 so that they produce more fetal hemoglobin, which compensates for the faulty adult version [36]. (The edit targets an erythroid-specific enhancer of the BCL11A gene.)

The pivotal trial results appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2024. In sickle cell disease, 44 patients received the treatment, and of 30 patients with enough follow-up to be evaluated, 29 (96.7%) had no severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 consecutive months, and all 30 were free of hospitalization for such crises over that period [36]. In transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, about 91% of evaluable patients reached transfusion independence [37]. The safety profile was consistent with the chemotherapy conditioning and stem-cell transplantation used, and no cancers were reported in these trial reports [36, 37].

The UK regulator approved it first, in late 2023, and the US FDA approved it for sickle cell disease in December 2023 and for transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia in January 2024 [36, 49]. It was the first approved therapy built on CRISPR. Cost has been a real obstacle: England's NICE issued draft guidance refusing it on cost-effectiveness grounds at one point in 2024, which patient charities contested [49]. The treatment also requires conditioning chemotherapy and specialist centers, which limits who can receive it.

In vivo: editing inside the body

In 2021 Gillmore and colleagues reported the first clinical data for a systemically delivered CRISPR therapy. NTLA-2001 packages Cas9 mRNA and a guide against the TTR gene in a lipid nanoparticle that goes to the liver, where it knocks out production of the misfolded transthyretin protein that causes ATTR amyloidosis. In six patients, the higher dose gave a mean reduction of about 87% in serum TTR [38].

The story since then is a useful reminder that early data are not the finish line. The drug (now called nexiguran ziclumeran, or nex-z) moved into Phase 3 trials. In October 2025, a patient in the MAGNITUDE trial developed Grade 4 liver transaminase elevations with raised bilirubin; the FDA placed clinical holds on both Phase 3 trials, and the patient later died of septic shock after a complicated course that the company said included acute liver injury [40]. The hold on MAGNITUDE-2 was lifted in January 2026 with enhanced liver monitoring [41], and the hold on MAGNITUDE was subsequently lifted too, with added liver monitoring, guidance on short-term steroids, and exclusion of patients with certain liver abnormalities [42]. The case shows that safety questions for in vivo editing are not hypothetical, and liver toxicity has been a recurring problem for gene therapies more broadly [42].

One patient, one therapy

In 2025 Musunuru, Ahrens-Nicklas and colleagues reported what is believed to be the first personalized in vivo base-editing therapy. An infant, known as KJ, was born with severe CPS1 deficiency, a urea-cycle disorder that stops the liver from clearing ammonia. Within roughly six months the team designed, made and obtained regulatory clearance for an adenine base editor delivered in lipid nanoparticles, targeting his specific mutation [39]. He received the first dose in February 2025 and further doses in March and April. As of the report he had no serious side effects, tolerated more dietary protein and needed less nitrogen-scavenging medication. The authors noted limitations: they could not take a liver biopsy to measure how many cells were corrected, and the results come from a single patient [39]. Even so, it shows how base editing and nanoparticle delivery could, in principle, let developers tailor treatments to ultra-rare mutations.

The hard parts

CRISPR is powerful, but it is not magic, and the limits are mostly well understood.

Off-target and unintended on-target edits. Cas9 can cut at sites that resemble the guide, and prediction software does not catch everything. Beyond small indels, editing can cause large deletions, translocations, inversions and even chromothripsis, which are harder to detect with standard sequencing workflows [43]. In therapy, regulators expect off-target assessment to be part of preclinical work, and a combination of prediction and unbiased experimental assays is used [32, 43]. Base and prime editors avoid double-strand breaks, which reduces some of these risks, but they have their own off-target profiles that continue to be studied [21].

Delivery. Getting the editor into the right cells is often the real bottleneck. Lipid nanoparticles reach the liver well and can be redosed, and their payload is transient. AAV vectors can reach other tissues but have limited cargo capacity and may persist long term [38, 43]. Reaching the brain, muscle or lungs efficiently remains an active research problem.

Precision of repair. HDR is inefficient in many cell types, which is part of why base and prime editing were developed [21].

Cost and access. Current approved therapies are complex and expensive, and the conditions they treat, such as sickle cell disease, are most common in places with limited access to specialist care [49].

Ethics and germline editing. Editing somatic cells, as in Casgevy, affects one patient. Editing embryos affects every cell and can be inherited. In 2018 He Jiankui announced that twin girls had been born from embryos he edited to confer HIV resistance. The scientific community condemned it almost universally, and he was sentenced to three years in prison in China [44]. Concerns raised include unintended edits and mosaicism, meaning not all cells carry the intended change [44]. Debates about whether and when heritable editing could ever be acceptable continue.

Where this leaves us

In about a decade and a half, CRISPR went from an oddity in yogurt-culture bacteria to a standard lab method and a licensed medicine. Its strength is that the part you change from experiment to experiment is a short piece of RNA, so the cost of asking a new question is low. Its weaknesses are also clear: delivery, safety monitoring and cost. Newer tools such as base editing and prime editing are aimed at the first two, and one-off therapies like KJ's hint at what could come if manufacturing and regulation can keep up.

If you are starting out, the practical lessons are simple. Design your guides with more than one tool, check every edit by sequencing, include proper controls, and be honest about what your assay can and cannot detect.
